name: Cannibal Rock
description: A seamount in Loh Dasami (Horseshoe Bay) at the far south of Komodo National Park, between Rinca and Nusa Kode. The pinnacle tops out around 4 m and drops past 35 m, its walls carpeted in Dendronephthya soft coral, crinoids, sponges, and tunicates. Cold upwelling feeds the south's signature critters: sea apples, frogfish, Bargibant's pygmy seahorses, and nudibranchs, with banded bamboo sharks tucked in ledges at night. Water runs green and plankton rich and can drop below 22 C mid year. The name comes from divers who watched one Komodo dragon eating another on the adjacent beach.
getThere: Fly to Labuan Bajo (LBJ / Komodo Airport) on Flores, with daily flights from Bali (DPS) and Jakarta (CGK). Cannibal Rock sits in the far south of the park, roughly 5-7 hours by boat from the harbour, so it is reached only on multi-day liveaboard south-circuit itineraries, not on day trips.

siteSpecificGear.name: 5mm wetsuit
siteSpecificGear.reason: South Komodo upwelling drives cold thermoclines that can drop below 22 C, especially June-September.

siteSpecificGear.name: Camera (macro) + dive light
siteSpecificGear.reason: The draw is small, cryptic critters on a soft-coral wall, often best worked on a slow or night dive.

notes: Liveaboard south circuit only; too far for day boats. Plankton-rich, low viz water and dense soft coral demand excellent buoyancy to avoid contact. Komodo dragons patrol the adjacent Horseshoe Bay beach.

name: Baixa do Ambrósio
description: An offshore seamount about 7 km north of Santa Maria that rises to within roughly 5 m of the surface and draws the Atlantic's largest known summer aggregation of sicklefin devil rays (Mobula tarapacana). From June to October, divers clip onto the mooring line at 5–15 m and watch groups of 10–30 golden backed rays, some with wingspans over 3 m, circle slowly in midwater alongside schooling almaco jacks and yellowmouth barracuda. Currents run moderate to strong, and late summer plankton blooms can bring whale sharks and oceanic mantas. A small platform sits near 40 m for experienced divers.

species.ecologicalDescription: The world's largest fish, reaching up to 12 metres, and entirely filter-feeding — no teeth, no threat to divers. Whale sharks congregate at predictable aggregation sites linked to seasonal plankton blooms and coral spawning events. Encounters typically involve slow surface swimming, allowing divers to pace alongside for extended periods. Their spotted pattern is unique to each individual, enabling photo-ID research. Listed as endangered; vessel strikes and fishing bycatch remain significant threats despite international protection.

getThere: Fly to Santa Maria Airport (SMA), usually connecting through Ponta Delgada (PDL) on São Miguel with Azores Airlines. Dive operators in Vila do Porto run boats to the seamount, roughly 7 km (about 3 nautical miles) off the island's north coast — a 30–45 minute crossing.

lodging.label: Hotel Praia de Lobos – Santa Maria

operators.label: Haliotis Dive Centre – Santa Maria, Azores

notes: Marine reserve: do not touch or chase the rays and stay on the mooring line. Offshore seamount exposed to current and surface chop, so a current experienced group is best. Devil ray sightings peak July–October and are never guaranteed.

name: Verde Island Drop-Off (San Agapito)
description: Off the south east corner of Verde Island, the San Agapito seamount rises in three peaks — the shallowest breaking the surface, the wall plunging past 70 metres into the Verde Island Passage, the strait a 2005 Carpenter–Springer study identified as the world's centre of marine shorefish biodiversity. Currents run hard here and can turn downward without warning, sweeping the rock in clouds of lyretail anthias while bigeye trevally, emperors and tuna patrol the blue. Gorgonian fans, 1.5-metre barrel sponges and volcanic gas bubbles seeping through the coral give the wall its texture; hawksbill turtles, frogfish and nudibranchs work the ledges. An advanced drift dive reached by banca from Puerto Galera.

species.ecologicalDescription: Schooling predators that form dense, swirling baitballs during the day at cleaning stations and reef edges — one of the most photogenic spectacles on Indo-Pacific reefs. The school rotates slowly, each fish orienting toward the current, creating a living silver cylinder that opens and closes around divers. At dusk, the school disperses and individuals hunt cooperatively across the reef flat. Their large eyes are adapted for low-light feeding. Bigeye trevally are important prey for large sharks and groupers, connecting mid-water and reef food webs.

One of the ocean's most visually striking reptiles, recognisable by its narrow, pointed beak and richly patterned shell. Hawksbills feed primarily on sponges, making them a keystone species on coral reefs — their grazing prevents sponges from overgrowing and smothering coral. Divers most often encounter them resting under coral ledges or methodically picking at reef walls. Critically endangered due to historical shell trade and ongoing egg harvesting, global populations have partially recovered in protected areas. Their presence is a strong indicator of a healthy, structurally complex reef.

getThere: Nearest major airport is Manila (MNL). Transfer to the Batangas pier and ferry to Puerto Galera (Sabang/Small La Laguna), the usual dive base; the Verde Island sites are about a 45-minute banca crossing from there, or roughly 2 hours by boat from Anilao.

lodging.label: El Galleon Beach Resort – Puerto Galera
Coco Beach Island Resort – Puerto Galera

notes: Advanced-only: currents are strong and unpredictable with frequent down currents, so a current experienced group, an SMB and a reef hook are recommended. Morning dives generally find the calmest seas. Part of the Verde Island Passage marine corridor.

name: Hikkaduwa Coral Sanctuary
description: Sri Lanka's first marine protected area — declared a sanctuary in 1979 and a marine national park in 2002 — fringing the beach town of Hikkaduwa on the southwest coast. The coral gardens sit in 3-12 m of warm, calm water 100-300 m offshore: a shallow fringing reef of Acropora tables, Montipora, and brain corals recovering from the 1998 bleaching and 2004 tsunami. Green and hawksbill turtles graze the heads daily and are reliably approachable, while parrotfish, surgeonfish, snappers, butterflyfish, Moorish idols, and moray eels work the coral, with the odd blacktip reef shark on the seaward edge. Shallow depth, easy shore and short boat access, and minimal current make it one of the island's best beginner and training reefs, busiest with glass bottom boats in the November-April dry season.

species.ecologicalDescription: One of the most wide-ranging marine reptiles, green turtles graze on seagrass and algae throughout tropical and subtropical seas. Unlike hawksbills, their diet means they are most often found near seagrass beds, sandy shallows, and reef flats, where they methodically crop vegetation. Divers typically encounter them resting on the seafloor or at cleaning stations where reef fish pick algae from their shells. Endangered; populations have recovered significantly at protected nesting beaches, though ocean plastic ingestion and boat strikes remain persistent threats.

Their presence is a strong indicator of a healthy, structurally complex reef.

The largest moray eel species, reaching up to 3 metres and commonly seen with just its head protruding from reef crevices, mouth opening and closing to pump oxygenated water over its gills — a behaviour often misread as aggression. Giant morays have poor eyesight and hunt by smell; they are not aggressive toward divers unless provoked or hand-fed. A cooperative hunting relationship with roving coral grouper has been documented, where grouper signal moray eels to flush prey from crevices. An ancient, alien-looking presence on any reef.

getThere: Fly into Colombo Bandaranaike International (CMB), then drive about 2.5 hours south to Hikkaduwa (100 km) on the Southern Expressway (E01), or take the scenic coastal train from Colombo Fort to Hikkaduwa station and a short tuk-tuk to the beach. The coral sanctuary lies directly off Hikkaduwa's main beach — dive centres run 5-10 minute boat trips and you can also snorkel in from shore. Conditions are reliable in the November-April dry season.

siteSpecificGear.name: Reef-safe sunscreen
siteSpecificGear.reason: The reef is shallow and heavily visited; reef-safe formulas reduce chemical load on already-stressed coral.

siteSpecificGear.name: SMB
siteSpecificGear.reason: Glass-bottom-boat and snorkel-tour traffic over the reef is constant in season — deploy an SMB and surface alert.

notes: The sanctuary lies within Hikkaduwa Marine National Park; a Department of Wildlife Conservation entry ticket applies and is usually arranged by dive operators. Coral here was hit hard by the 1998 mass bleaching and the 2004 tsunami and is still recovering — do not touch or stand on coral, and do not chase or ride turtles. Boat and snorkel tour traffic over the shallow reef is heavy, so dive on a deployed SMB. Diving turns rough and visibility collapses during the May-September southwest monsoon.

name: Dos Amigos Grande
description: The larger of two rock spires that break the surface off the exposed southwest corner of Cocos. The signature dive is the cleaning station near 30 m, one of the few spots at Cocos where scalloped hammerheads hang almost motionless while barberfish and king angelfish pick them over — the sharks held still rather than passing in the blue. Ascending the reef, a rock archway rises to within about 18 m of the surface, framing whitetip reef sharks, marble rays, green turtles, and schools of jacks and snapper. Current strengthens toward the shallows.

species.ecologicalDescription: Iconic for their laterally-extended cephalofoil — the hammer-shaped head that improves electroreception and manoeuvrability — scalloped hammerheads are pelagic schooling sharks most often encountered at seamounts and offshore pinnacles. Schools of dozens to hundreds form at depth during the day, dispersing at night to hunt. The hammer provides a 360-degree vertical field of vision, making them acutely aware of divers. Critically endangered; fins are among the most traded shark products globally, and populations have collapsed at many historical aggregation sites.

A slender, nocturnal predator instantly identified by the white tips on its dorsal and caudal fins. During the day, whitetips rest motionless in groups on sandy ledges or inside reef caves — divers frequently swim directly over resting aggregations. At night they become highly active hunters, pursuing fish and octopus through reef crevices with remarkable agility. Unlike many sharks, they are non-territorial toward divers and typically ignore human presence. Listed as vulnerable; their slow reproductive rate makes populations sensitive to fishing pressure.

Endangered; populations have recovered significantly at protected nesting beaches, though ocean plastic ingestion and boat strikes remain persistent threats.

Bigeye trevally are important prey for large sharks and groupers, connecting mid-water and reef food webs.

getThere: San José (SJO) is Costa Rica's main international airport. Cocos is reached only by liveaboard from Puntarenas, a roughly 36-hour open-ocean crossing each way; trips run 8-11 days.

siteSpecificGear.name: Temperate-grade wetsuit
siteSpecificGear.reason: Thermoclines can drop water to around 19-22°C at the cleaning-station depth even in the warm season.

siteSpecificGear.name: Reef hook
siteSpecificGear.reason: Hooking in on the up-current side lets you hold position and watch the hammerheads being cleaned.

siteSpecificGear.name: Nitrox certification
siteSpecificGear.reason: Most operators run nitrox to extend bottom time on the repeated 30 m profiles.

notes: Permit-controlled national park; liveaboard only access. The site sits off the exposed southwest corner of the island and can be surgy with strong, shifting current.

name: Drop-Off (Sipadan)
description: Sipadan's house reef: the crest sits in 3-5m of water before the wall falls vertically toward 600m down the flank of the drowned volcano that Jacques Cousteau's 1989 film 'Borneo: The Ghost of the Sea Turtle' put on the map. Green turtles are the constant here - they graze the wall and rest on ledges in the shallows, often a dozen in sight at once - joined by hawksbill turtles, whitetip reef sharks, and passing schools of bigeye trevally and bumphead parrotfish. The shallow shelf makes it the island's gentlest entry, but the drop is sheer and current can build along the lip.

species.ecologicalDescription: A large, air-breathing reptile that returns to the same nesting beaches generation after generation. Divers encounter green sea turtles resting under coral ledges, cruising reef edges, or feeding on algae and seagrass. They are often habituated to slow-moving divers at popular sites. Their slow growth rate — taking 20–50 years to reach sexual maturity — means that even small levels of adult mortality have outsized population impacts. Endangered globally but recovering in regions with strong nesting beach protection.

Hawksbills feed primarily on sponges, making them a keystone species on coral reefs — their grazing prevents sponges from overgrowing and smothering coral. Critically endangered due to historical shell trade and ongoing egg harvesting, global populations have partially recovered in protected areas. Their presence is a strong indicator of a healthy, structurally complex reef.

getThere: Fly to Tawau (TWU) in Sabah from Kuala Lumpur or Kota Kinabalu, transfer by road to Semporna (about 1.5 hours), then take a dive-boat to Sipadan (roughly 60 minutes). No accommodation exists on Sipadan itself - divers stay on nearby Mabul, Kapalai, or Mataking and day-trip to the island.
notes: A daily Sabah Parks permit is required - only 176 are issued per day across all operators, so book a multi day package months ahead. No overnight stays on the island; touching or feeding marine life is prohibited inside the marine park.

name: HMS Southwold
description: The HMS Southwold, a Type II Hunt-class destroyer, lies in two main sections off the coast of Malta, a victim of a German mine in March 1942. This WWII naval wreck provides a dramatic historical dive, offering a glimpse into the past. Advanced divers can explore the remains of this significant vessel, now home to a variety of Mediterranean marine life.
getThere: Fly to Malta International Airport (MLA), then take a ferry or boat to Gozo. The wreck is accessed by dive boat.
notes: Due to depth, this site is suitable for advanced or technical divers. Standard diving permits and regulations apply.

name: HMCS Chaudiere
description: The HMCS Chaudiere is a captivating artificial reef off the coast of British Columbia, offering divers a chance to explore a deliberately sunk warship. This former destroyer escort provides habitat for a diverse array of cold water marine life, including various rockfish, lingcod, and colorful anemones. Its accessible depth and intriguing structure make it a popular site for advanced divers seeking a historical and ecological adventure in the Pacific Northwest.
getThere: Accessible from Nanaimo, British Columbia, by local dive charter boats.

lodging.label: Inn at Laurel Point – Victoria, BC

operators.label: Ogden Point Dive Centre – Victoria, BC

notes: Subject to local currents and tides; consult with local dive operators for optimal dive times.

name: Bangaram Atoll
description: Bangaram Atoll, an uninhabited jewel in Lakshadweep, India, offers a pristine underwater experience with vibrant coral reefs surrounding a shallow lagoon. Divers can explore healthy reef systems teeming with diverse marine life, including various reef fish, turtles, and rays. The atoll's clear waters and untouched environment provide an intimate encounter with nature.
getThere: Fly to Agatti Airport (AGX) in Lakshadweep, then transfer to Bangaram Atoll by speedboat (approximately 20-30 minutes). Flights to Agatti are typically from Kochi (COK).

operators.label: CGH Earth Bangaram Island Dive Centre

notes: All visitors to Lakshadweep require an entry permit from the Lakshadweep Administration. Foreign nationals also need additional clearances. Ensure all permits are secured well in advance of travel.

name: Bay of Pigs
description: The Bay of Pigs is a renowned dive site in Cuba, famous for its calm, clear waters and vibrant marine ecosystem. Divers can explore a dramatic wall that drops to over 30 meters, alongside various cenotes and caverns. The site is home to diverse marine life, including barracudas, tarpon, and eagle rays, making it a popular destination for both scuba diving and snorkeling.
getThere: Nearest airport is Abel Santamaría Airport (SNU) in Santa Clara, about 1.5-2 hours drive. Viazul buses and taxis are available to Giron or Playa Larga near Bay of Pigs.

lodging.label: Hotel Playa Girón – Bay of Pigs
Villa Playa Larga – Bay of Pigs
Avalon Aggressor – Jardines de la Reina Liveaboard

name: Capurgana
description: Capurgana offers a tranquil diving experience in the Colombian Caribbean, characterized by vibrant coral reefs and a rich diversity of macro life. Divers can explore shallow coral gardens and deeper walls, encountering colorful reef fish, crustaceans, and occasional pelagic visitors. The clear, warm waters provide excellent visibility for exploring the healthy ecosystems.
getThere: Accessible by boat from Turbo or Necoclí, Colombia. Nearest major airport is in Medellín (MDE) or Cartagena (CTG), followed by domestic flight or bus to Turbo/Necoclí.

name: Cuba Jardines de la Reina
description: Jardines de la Reina, or Gardens of the Queen, is a protected marine park off the southern coast of Cuba. This pristine archipelago offers vibrant coral reefs, dramatic wall dives, and consistent encounters with resident Caribbean reef sharks and silvertip sharks. Known for its healthy ecosystem, divers can observe large groupers, schooling snappers, and a rich diversity of marine life in clear, warm waters.

species.ecologicalDescription: The dominant large shark on Caribbean coral reefs, characterised by a stocky build and rounded snout. Caribbean reef sharks patrol reef edges and drop-offs, often in loose groups, and are the species most commonly encountered in Caribbean shark dives. They are opportunistic predators of fish and cephalopods, and play a critical top-down regulatory role on the reef. Near threatened; heavily fished for fins and meat across their range. At sites with dive tourism value, local protection has allowed populations to partially recover.

getThere: Fly to Cayo Coco (CCC) or Camagüey (CMW), then transfer by bus to Júcaro, followed by a liveaboard boat to Jardines de la Reina.

lodging.label: Jardines de la Reina Liveaboards – liveaboard.com

operators.label: Jardines de la Reina Diving – PADI Travel

notes: Access to Jardines de la Reina is restricted to liveaboard operations with special permits. Fishing is strictly prohibited.

name: Kadmat Island
description: Kadmat Island offers diverse coral reef diving in the pristine waters of Lakshadweep. Known for its healthy hard and soft corals, the sites attract a variety of reef fish, pelagic species, and occasional encounters with sharks and turtles. The calm conditions and clear visibility make it suitable for all levels of divers.
getThere: Fly to Kochi (COK) or Chennai (MAA), then a domestic flight to Agatti (AGX). From Agatti, take a ferry or speed boat to Kadmat Island. Permits are required for travel to Lakshadweep.
notes: Access to Lakshadweep requires special permits from the Indian government, which are usually arranged by tour operators. Marine park rules apply.

name: Memba Bay
description: Memba Bay offers a glimpse into the diverse marine ecosystems of northern Mozambique, characterized by vibrant coral formations and a variety of tropical fish. The bay's sheltered waters provide conditions suitable for a range of dive experiences.
getThere: Access via Nacala Airport (MNC) with onward transfer by road and boat.

name: Museo Atlantico
description: Museo Atlantico is Europe's only underwater museum, located off the coast of Lanzarote, Spain. It features a series of thought provoking sculptures by artist Jason deCaires Taylor, designed to create an artificial reef and a powerful message about marine conservation. Divers can explore various installations including a 'Rubicon' of human figures, the 'Jellyfish Tree', and 'The Raft of Lampedusa', experiencing art and nature in a unique submerged gallery.
getThere: Fly into Arrecife Airport (ACE) in Lanzarote, then drive or take a taxi to Playa Blanca. Dive operators offer boat trips to the museum.
notes: Access to Museo Atlantico is typically through authorized dive centers only. Permits are required and usually arranged by the dive operator. Respect the art installations and marine life.

name: Punta Cana
description: Punta Cana offers a range of shallow reef dives and some deeper sites with vibrant coral formations. Marine life includes various reef fish and occasional larger pelagics like nurse sharks and stingrays. Expect clear waters and gentle currents on most dives.
getThere: Fly into Punta Cana International Airport (PUJ). Many dive operators offer transfers from local resorts.

lodging.label: Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Punta Cana
Be Live Experience Hamaca – Boca Chica

notes: Popular for resort diving, with a mix of artificial reefs and natural formations.

name: Taganga
description: Taganga is a traditional fishing village on Colombia's Caribbean coast, a popular entry point for divers exploring the nearby reefs. The calm bay offers accessible dive sites with a variety of coral formations and diverse macro life, making it suitable for all skill levels from beginners to experienced divers.
getThere: Nearest airport is Simón Bolívar International Airport (SMR) in Santa Marta. From there, take a taxi or bus to Taganga (approx. 10-15 minutes).

name: Blue Hole Gozo
description: An iconic dive site near Dwejra Bay on Gozo, known for its dramatic underwater archways and rock formations. Divers enter a natural rock pool and descend into the open sea, exploring caves and crevices. The site offers a unique geological experience with abundant marine life.
getThere: Fly to Malta International Airport (MLA), then take a ferry to Mġarr Harbour in Gozo. The site is accessible from Dwejra Bay by car.

name: Ghar Qawqla
description: Ghar Qawqla offers a unique cave diving experience on Gozo, Malta, with fascinating rock formations and calm, clear waters. Divers can explore the illuminated cavern entrance and discover a variety of macro life clinging to the walls and crevices.
getThere: Accessible from various dive centers across Gozo. Usually reached by boat or shore entry depending on specific site conditions.
notes: Always dive with a guide familiar with Gozo's cave systems.

name: Inland Sea Gozo
description: The Inland Sea in Gozo offers a unique diving experience, starting in a shallow lagoon and leading through a natural tunnel to the open sea. Divers can explore rock formations and a vibrant ecosystem in sheltered conditions.
getThere: Fly to Malta International Airport (MLA), then take a ferry from Cirkewwa (Malta) to Mgarr (Gozo). The Inland Sea is located near Dwejra Bay on Gozo.
notes: Entrance is through a natural tunnel, conditions inside the Inland Sea are usually calm. Can be crowded during peak season.

name: Jellyfish Lake
description: A marine lake on Eil Malk island in the southern Rock Islands, cut off from the sea since the last ice age and reached by a short climb over a limestone ridge from the boat landing. Snorkelers cross water thick with golden jellyfish (Mastigias papua etpisoni), an endemic subspecies that lost most of its sting in isolation and pulses across the lake each day to keep its symbiotic algae in sunlight. Moon jellyfish drift through the same surface layer. Scuba is banned: exhaled bubbles lodge under the bells and harm the animals, and a hydrogen sulfide layer below 15 m is dangerous to breathe near. Golden jellyfish numbers swing with climate, from tens of millions in good years to near total collapse and back.
getThere: Koror (ROR / Roman Tmetuchl International) is Palau's only international airport, with flights from Manila, Taipei, Seoul, Guam, and Tokyo. The lake sits on Eil Malk island in the southern Rock Islands, roughly a 45 minute boat ride south of Koror followed by a short uphill climb over the ridge to the water. Most Koror day boats include it on a Rock Islands snorkel itinerary.

siteSpecificGear.name: Snorkel and mask (no scuba)
siteSpecificGear.reason: Scuba is prohibited in the lake; the visit is a surface snorkel, so mask, snorkel and fins are all you take in.

siteSpecificGear.name: Rash guard
siteSpecificGear.reason: A thin layer guards skin against incidental contact with the mild jellyfish and against sun on the long surface swim.

notes: Permits: requires the Rock Islands / Koror State permit plus a separate Jellyfish Lake permit, usually bundled by operators with the Palau Pristine Paradise Environmental Fee paid on arrival. Snorkel only, no scuba. Rinse off sunscreen and oils before entering to protect the lake. Golden jellyfish densities have crashed and recovered repeatedly with El Niño warming, so the spectacle varies widely by year; confirm current status before booking.

name: Numidia Wreck
description: A 137 m Anchor Line steamer that ran straight onto the north point of Big Brother in July 1901 and slid down the reef wall, where she now lies almost vertical — bow at 8 m, stern past 80 m. Two railway axles and their iron wheels still sit on the deck near 25 m, cargo that never reached Calcutta. Soft corals and gorgonians sheath the hull, clouds of glassfish fill the holds, and anthias hang over the rails while grey reef sharks patrol the blue off the stern.

species.ecologicalDescription: One of the Indo-Pacific's most abundant reef sharks and a defining presence on healthy coral reefs. Grey reef sharks are mid-water patrollers, typically seen in small groups or alone along reef edges and drop-offs. They are curious rather than aggressive, often circling divers at a consistent distance. A distinctive threat display — arched back, depressed pectoral fins, exaggerated swimming — signals discomfort if divers approach too closely. Near threatened; their numbers have declined sharply in areas with intensive fishing.

Among the largest bony fish on coral reefs, male Napoleon wrasse (also called humphead wrasse) can reach 2 metres and are unmistakable: a steep forehead hump, thick fleshy lips, and vivid blue-green patterning. They feed on hard-shelled invertebrates including sea urchins and crown-of-thorns starfish, playing an important regulatory role on reefs. Solitary and slow-moving, they are often habituated to divers at popular sites. Endangered globally due to targeted fishing for the live reef food fish trade.

getThere: Liveaboard-only, departing Hurghada (HRG) or Marsa Alam (RMF), both with direct European flights. Southern itineraries that take in Brothers, Daedalus and Elphinstone run roughly 5 to 7 nights and reach the El Ikhwa (Brother) Islands offshore in the central Red Sea.

lodging.label: MY Blue Melody – Red Sea Liveaboard

notes: The wreck drops down a vertical wall: bow around 8 m, the railway wheels near 25 m, midship by 40 to 50 m and the stern beyond 80 m, so the lower hull is technical only. Brother Islands are liveaboard only and the marine park is generally reachable only in the calmer months.

name: Bimini Great Hammerheads
description: From December to March, great hammerheads up to 4 m long patrol a shallow white sand flat on the lee side of South Bimini, the most reliable encounter with this species anywhere in the Atlantic. Divers kneel on the bottom at around 6 m while a baited handler draws the sharks in to glide past at arm's length, scalloped heads sweeping the sand. Nurse sharks and wintering bull sharks crowd the same flat, and the Gulf Stream runs along the deep edge just offshore. Visibility stays high over the pale sand, making this one of the great wide angle shark photography dives.

species.ecologicalDescription: Bottom-dwelling, largely nocturnal sharks that spend much of the day resting in groups under coral ledges or on sandy substrate. Nurse sharks are identifiable by their broad, flattened heads, small eyes, and twin nasal barbels used to sense prey in sand and rubble. They feed on crustaceans, molluscs, and small fish, using powerful suction to extract prey from crevices. Among the least threatening sharks to divers — slow-moving, benign, and tolerant of close approach when resting. They should not be handled; bites from provoked individuals, while rare, are powerful.

The dominant large shark on Caribbean coral reefs, characterised by a stocky build and rounded snout. Caribbean reef sharks patrol reef edges and drop-offs, often in loose groups, and are the species most commonly encountered in Caribbean shark dives. They are opportunistic predators of fish and cephalopods, and play a critical top-down regulatory role on the reef. Near threatened; heavily fished for fins and meat across their range. At sites with dive tourism value, local protection has allowed populations to partially recover.

getThere: South Bimini Airport (BIM) is a 25 minute flight from Fort Lauderdale, or reach Bimini by fast ferry from Miami. The hammerhead flat is a short boat ride on the lee side of South Bimini, about 5 minutes from the island resorts and dive centers.

siteSpecificGear.name: 5mm wetsuit
siteSpecificGear.reason: Divers kneel still on the sand for the whole dive; winter water near 23C chills you without the extra neoprene.

siteSpecificGear.name: Wide angle camera
siteSpecificGear.reason: Four metre hammerheads pass within arm's reach over bright sand, the classic close focus wide angle shot.

notes: Baited, guided shark dive run by Bimini operators; the great hammerhead season runs roughly November to April and peaks January to March. Expect a long, shallow dive kneeling on sand while sharks are drawn in with bait. Nurse and bull sharks share the site, and a Gulf Stream current runs along the nearby drop. This is a pelagic encounter dive, not a reef or coral site.

name: Manta Ray Night Dive (Garden Eel Cove)
description: By day this sandy shelf off Keahole Point is Garden Eel Cove, named for the colonies of Hawaiian garden eels that sway from the bottom near 12 m. After dark it becomes Manta Heaven: crews set powerful lights on the sand at about 11 m, the glow concentrates plankton into a bright column, and resident reef mantas with wingspans near 4 m sweep in to barrel roll through the swarm, mouths agape, sometimes passing inches above kneeling divers. Kona's catalog holds more than 200 identified individuals, so the show runs most nights of the year. A resident undulated moray nicknamed Frank often turns up to pick off fish drawn to the lights. Keahole Point shelters the cove from the summer south swell.

species.ecologicalDescription: The smaller of the two manta species, with wingspans reaching up to 5 metres, reef mantas are filter-feeders tied to specific cleaning stations and feeding aggregation sites. Divers who approach cleaning stations — typically coral bommies swarming with wrasse — often witness mantas hovering motionless as cleaner fish pick parasites from their gills and skin. Cephalic fins — the horn-like lobes that give mantas their informal name — are used to funnel plankton-rich water into their mouths during feeding. Vulnerable; slow to reproduce and heavily targeted for gill plate in traditional medicine.

getThere: Fly into Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport (KOA) at Keahole, minutes from the site. Manta night dive boats leave Honokohau Harbor just north of Kailua Kona and reach Garden Eel Cove in 20 to 30 minutes. The Keauhou Bay site, known as Manta Village, is the alternate to the south when swell favors it. Shore entry over lava rock is possible but most divers go by boat.

lodging.label: Four Seasons Resort Hualalai at Historic Ka'upulehu
Courtyard by Marriott King Kamehameha's Kona Beach Hotel
Sheraton Kona Resort & Spa at Keauhou Bay

operators.label: Jack's Diving Locker – Manta Ray Night Dive
Fair Wind Cruises – Manta Night Dive

siteSpecificGear.name: Backup dive light
siteSpecificGear.reason: Every diver carries a primary and a backup light for the night descent, even though crews set the big plankton lights on the sand.

siteSpecificGear.name: 5mm wetsuit
siteSpecificGear.reason: You kneel motionless on the sand for 30 to 45 minutes while the mantas feed, so divers chill faster than the warm water suggests, especially on winter nights.

notes: This is a night dive: bring a primary and backup light, though operators supply the bottom lights that draw the plankton. The dive is shallow and stationary, so divers get cold quickly. Touching mantas is prohibited and strips their protective mucus; stay low, keep your arms in, and let them pass over you. Garden Eel Cove off the airport is the more sheltered choice in summer, while Keauhou Bay can be exposed to south swell.

name: Garden of Eden
description: A wall and coral plateau off the western tip of Qesmah, one of the nine Daymaniyat islands scattered 70 km off Muscat. Boulders and blocks spangled with orange, purple and yellow soft corals drop from a 12 m shelf to sand near 23 m. Green and hawksbill turtles graze the plateau, which sits inside a reserve set aside in 1996 to protect their nesting beaches, and whale sharks cruise through on the late summer plankton bloom.

species.ecologicalDescription: One of the ocean's most visually striking reptiles, recognisable by its narrow, pointed beak and richly patterned shell. Hawksbills feed primarily on sponges, making them a keystone species on coral reefs — their grazing prevents sponges from overgrowing and smothering coral. Divers most often encounter them resting under coral ledges or methodically picking at reef walls. Critically endangered due to historical shell trade and ongoing egg harvesting, global populations have partially recovered in protected areas. Their presence is a strong indicator of a healthy, structurally complex reef.

One of the most wide-ranging marine reptiles, green turtles graze on seagrass and algae throughout tropical and subtropical seas. Unlike hawksbills, their diet means they are most often found near seagrass beds, sandy shallows, and reef flats, where they methodically crop vegetation. Divers typically encounter them resting on the seafloor or at cleaning stations where reef fish pick algae from their shells. Endangered; populations have recovered significantly at protected nesting beaches, though ocean plastic ingestion and boat strikes remain persistent threats.

The world's largest fish, reaching up to 12 metres, and entirely filter-feeding — no teeth, no threat to divers. Whale sharks congregate at predictable aggregation sites linked to seasonal plankton blooms and coral spawning events. Encounters typically involve slow surface swimming, allowing divers to pace alongside for extended periods. Their spotted pattern is unique to each individual, enabling photo-ID research. Listed as endangered; vessel strikes and fishing bycatch remain significant threats despite international protection.

Elegant, wing-shaped rays recognised by a white-spotted black dorsum and a long, whip-like tail. Spotted eagle rays are active swimmers, covering large distances in open water and occasionally forming large feeding schools. They prey on buried molluscs and crustaceans, using their flat, plate-like teeth to crush shells. Often encountered cruising along reef edges or in blue water above the reef. Near threatened globally; highly susceptible to bycatch. A highlight of any dive — their wing-beat motion in open water is one of the ocean's most graceful sights.

getThere: Fly into Muscat International (MCT), Oman's main hub with direct links across Europe, Asia and the Gulf. Dive boats run out to the islands in about 60 to 90 minutes from marinas just north of the city, such as Al Mouj and Seeb.

lodging.label: Al Bandar Hotel – Shatti Al Qurum Muscat

notes: The Daymaniyat Islands are a protected nature reserve. Landing is closed during turtle and seabird nesting season (roughly May to October), and all diving must be booked through licensed Muscat operators. Carry an SMB for boat traffic inside the reserve.

name: San Miguel Island
description: San Miguel is the westernmost and most exposed of the Channel Islands, where the cold California Current slams into the coast and feeds dense giant kelp. Point Bennett on the western tip holds the largest pinniped haul out on the planet, with California and Steller sea lions, northern fur seals, harbor seals and elephant seals piled by the thousand. Drop into the kelp off Tyler Bight and curious young sea lions corkscrew through the golden canopy at arm's length. The classic dive is Wyckoff Ledge, a rock wall falling from 12 m to a sand floor near 27 m and crusted with strawberry anemones, nudibranchs, wolf eels and lingcod. Water hovers around 11 to 13 C and the seas are unforgiving, so the island only opens on calm days.

getThere: Fly into Santa Barbara (SBA) or Los Angeles (LAX). Dive boats run from Santa Barbara Harbor and Ventura Harbor. San Miguel is the most distant of the Channel Islands, a crossing of roughly 3 to 5 hours, so it is almost always reached on multi day liveaboard charters rather than day trips. There are no facilities on the island.
notes: Part of Channel Islands National Park and National Marine Sanctuary; the island is owned by the US Navy and managed by the National Park Service. Going ashore needs a permit and a ranger escort, and Point Bennett is closed to protect breeding wildlife, so the diving is done from the boat offshore. Conditions are exposed with strong swell and current and the island is frequently weathered out, calmest from late summer into fall. Cold water calls for a 7mm wetsuit with hood and gloves or a drysuit. Never approach hauled out pinnipeds.

name: Peleliu Corner
description: Peleliu marks the southern tip of Palau's barrier reef, where Pacific Ocean and Philippine Sea currents collide over a submarine ridge between Peleliu and Angaur, generating some of the strongest flow in Palau. The dive traces the sheer Peleliu Wall, dropping past giant sea fans from a 10 m plateau near the World War II landing beach monument to a 30 m corner where Peleliu Cut and Peleliu Express merge. Divers set a reef hook at the lip and hold against the rip while grey reef sharks cruise the blue in groups of 15 or more, joined by whitetips, bumphead parrotfish, Napoleon wrasse, and schooling barracuda. Slack tide windows are short and the current can pull divers deep into the corner, so trips are timed to the tide tables. Sailfin snapper mass to spawn here from March through May.

species.ecologicalDescription: One of the Indo-Pacific's most abundant reef sharks and a defining presence on healthy coral reefs. Grey reef sharks are mid-water patrollers, typically seen in small groups or alone along reef edges and drop-offs. They are curious rather than aggressive, often circling divers at a consistent distance. A distinctive threat display — arched back, depressed pectoral fins, exaggerated swimming — signals discomfort if divers approach too closely. Near threatened; their numbers have declined sharply in areas with intensive fishing.

A slender, nocturnal predator instantly identified by the white tips on its dorsal and caudal fins. During the day, whitetips rest motionless in groups on sandy ledges or inside reef caves — divers frequently swim directly over resting aggregations. At night they become highly active hunters, pursuing fish and octopus through reef crevices with remarkable agility. Unlike many sharks, they are non-territorial toward divers and typically ignore human presence. Listed as vulnerable; their slow reproductive rate makes populations sensitive to fishing pressure.

Among the largest bony fish on coral reefs, male Napoleon wrasse (also called humphead wrasse) can reach 2 metres and are unmistakable: a steep forehead hump, thick fleshy lips, and vivid blue-green patterning. They feed on hard-shelled invertebrates including sea urchins and crown-of-thorns starfish, playing an important regulatory role on reefs. Solitary and slow-moving, they are often habituated to divers at popular sites. Endangered globally due to targeted fishing for the live reef food fish trade.

Iconic for their laterally-extended cephalofoil — the hammer-shaped head that improves electroreception and manoeuvrability — scalloped hammerheads are pelagic schooling sharks most often encountered at seamounts and offshore pinnacles. Schools of dozens to hundreds form at depth during the day, dispersing at night to hunt. The hammer provides a 360-degree vertical field of vision, making them acutely aware of divers. Critically endangered; fins are among the most traded shark products globally, and populations have collapsed at many historical aggregation sites.

getThere: Fly into Roman Tmetuchl International Airport (ROR) near Koror via Manila, Taipei, Tokyo, or Guam. Peleliu lies about 56 km south of Koror at the bottom of the barrier reef; most divers reach it on a long speedboat run from Koror or by liveaboard working the southern reefs, while a small island airfield and ferry serve those staying on Peleliu itself.

siteSpecificGear.name: Reef hook
siteSpecificGear.reason: Currents are among the strongest in Palau and reverse at the tide change. Hooking into rubble at the 10 to 15 m lip is the only way to hold position and watch the shark line without finning hard.

siteSpecificGear.name: Surface marker buoy
siteSpecificGear.reason: Drift exits run out over open ocean off the corner, so operators require an SMB deployed on ascent for boat pickup.

notes: Permit: Koror State Rock Islands pass plus the Palau Pristine Paradise Environmental Fee, paid on arrival. Advanced certification with drift and reef hook experience expected. Currents are tide driven and can run hard with strong downcurrents near the corner, so dives are scheduled around slack water; follow the tide and exit briefing closely. Often combined with WWII wreck dives and topside battlefield visits.

name: Rainbow Warrior
description: Greenpeace's flagship, bombed by French secret service agents in Auckland Harbour in 1985 in an attack that killed photographer Fernando Pereira, now rests off the Cavalli Islands near Matauri Bay. The salvaged hull was scuttled here in December 1987 as an artificial reef, the masts removed and displayed onshore. The 40 m wreck lies upright in 27 m of water with the deck around 16 m, its steel skin smothered in a dense carpet of varicoloured jewel anemones that give the dive its nickname, Jewel of the North. Schools of snapper, blue maomao and demoiselles hang over the wreck while kingfish patrol the blue and john dory hover near the superstructure. Cooler subtropical water and depth make this an advanced dive, though current is usually mild.
getThere: Fly into Auckland or Kerikeri (Bay of Islands), then drive to Matauri Bay or Tutukaka in Northland. Dive charters run to the wreck from Matauri Bay (about 10 minutes by boat to the Cavalli Islands) and on day trips from Paihia and Tutukaka.

operators.label: PADI Travel – Poor Knights New Zealand

notes: The wreck lies within a marine area managed as a fish sanctuary; no fishing or souvenir collecting. Depth to 27 m and cool water make this an advanced dive; penetration of the hull requires wreck training and a guide. Surface conditions in exposed Northland water can build quickly, so trips depend on weather windows.

name: Saco do Cardeiro
description: A sheltered cove on the calm inner sea of Arraial do Cabo, the mar de dentro, where a rocky bottom slopes gently from about 6 to 11 meters under unusually clear water. Cold, plankton rich pulses from the South Atlantic upwelling feed dense schools of bigeye and other fish that drift over reef carpeted in zoanthids, gorgonians and sponges. Divers come for the resident longsnout seahorses and for a bright orange and pink soft coral, not native to Brazil, that has colonised the rocks and become a favorite subject for underwater photographers. Barracuda, green turtles, small morays and the occasional dolphin pass through. Gentle depth and protected water make this Arraial's main training and discover scuba site.

species.ecologicalDescription: A solitary apex predator with a reputation exceeding its actual threat to divers. Great barracuda are ambush hunters, hovering motionless in mid-water before striking fish at high speed using rows of razor-sharp teeth. Their habit of following divers — likely investigating the reflection and movement of equipment — can feel intimidating but is almost always investigative rather than aggressive. They reach up to 1.8 metres. Flesh can carry ciguatera toxin in tropical regions; recreational encounters are considered low risk.

A large, air-breathing reptile that returns to the same nesting beaches generation after generation. Divers encounter green sea turtles resting under coral ledges, cruising reef edges, or feeding on algae and seagrass. They are often habituated to slow-moving divers at popular sites. Their slow growth rate — taking 20–50 years to reach sexual maturity — means that even small levels of adult mortality have outsized population impacts. Endangered globally but recovering in regions with strong nesting beach protection.

getThere: Fly into Cabo Frio Airport (CFB), about 25 minutes by road, or Rio de Janeiro Galeao (GIG), roughly 2.5 hours by car or bus. Dive boats leave the Praia dos Anjos pier in Arraial do Cabo; the cove is about a 15 minute ride into the sheltered inner sea.

operators.label: PADI Travel – Arraial do Cabo Brazil

notes: Shallow, sheltered cove that operators use for discover scuba and certification dives, so expect training groups. Departures are by boat from the Praia dos Anjos pier, and the area lies within the Arraial do Cabo Marine Extractive Reserve. Water can cool sharply when upwelling drives cold water inshore, even in Brazilian summer, so carry enough exposure protection.

name: Boiler Wreck (Abu Madafi)
description: Abu Madafi is an offshore reef about 30 minutes by boat north of Jeddah, and its signature dive is the Boiler Wreck, a steamer that has lain here so long that little remains beyond a section of the stern and the two heavy iron boilers it is named for, now thickly crusted in hard and soft coral. The wreckage rests in 4 to 20 meters on a reef pierced by a network of caves and narrow passages where shafts of sunlight cut through openings overhead, and a coral wall drops away alongside into deeper water. Moderate current pulls in whitetip and blacktip reef sharks, great barracuda, dogtooth tuna and jacks, with reef mantas passing through in the cooler months. It is the most dived site in Jeddah and an approachable introduction to Saudi Red Sea diving.

getThere: Fly into King Abdulaziz International Airport (JED) in Jeddah. Dive operators run boats from the marinas at Obhur (Sharm Obhur) on the northern edge of the city, and it is roughly a 30 minute ride out to the Abu Madafi reef.

operators.label: PADI Travel – Saudi Arabia Red Sea

notes: Boat dive on an open reef with moderate current, so it suits divers comfortable with mild drift. Several wrecks lie on Abu Madafi besides the Boiler Wreck, including the Old Coaster and the Pipe Wreck, and the reef is riddled with caves and passages that reward good buoyancy and a torch. Coordinates are approximate for an offshore reef reached by boat from Obhur. Diving in Saudi Arabia is arranged through licensed local operators.

name: Crystal Rock
description: A current swept pinnacle in the far north of Komodo National Park, 300 m from Castle Rock, rising from open water to break the surface at low tide. A submerged spur falls away to a saddle near 20 m, its walls stacked with giant sea fans, barrel sponges, and soft coral in reds and orange. The water is famously clear, often well past 25 m, which is how the site earned its name. When the tide runs, grey reef and whitetip sharks hold in the flow on the up current side while clouds of fusiliers, snapper, and surgeonfish wrap the slopes and anthias swarm the shallows. Plate corals around 17 m shelter resting whitetip pups.

Encountered singly or in small groups near reef passes and current-exposed structures, they actively pursue and herd prey fish. GTs are highly aware of divers and often use them as cover to ambush fish disturbed by human movement — a well-documented hunting adaptation. Prized game fish; populations have declined on heavily fished reefs.

getThere: Fly into Labuan Bajo (LBJ / Komodo Airport) on Flores, which has multiple daily domestic flights from Bali (DPS) and Jakarta (CGK). Crystal Rock lies in the far north of the park near Gili Lawa, roughly 3 to 4 hours by fast day boat from Labuan Bajo harbour and most often dived as a stop on a Komodo liveaboard.

siteSpecificGear.name: Reef hook
siteSpecificGear.reason: The crown of the seamount sits in ripping current, and hooking into bare reef is the only way to hold position while the sharks and schooling fish stream past.

siteSpecificGear.name: SMB and reel
siteSpecificGear.reason: Drift exits put you over open water, so send a marker buoy up before you ascend.

notes: Negative entry and consistently strong current make this an advanced dive, not a spot for new divers. Surface on the down current side and never up current of the rock. Komodo National Park entry and ranger fees apply, and most divers reach the far north on a liveaboard rather than a day boat.

name: Balun
description: Balun is a wall dive on the open Adriatic flank of the northern Kornati islands, where the archipelago's limestone crowns drop from the surface into deep blue water. Finning southeast along the cliff, divers reach a terrace near 26 metres where the rock turns thick with red and violet gorgonian sea fans (Paramuricea clavata) and golden Eunicella, packed among yellow sulphur sponges at a density rarely seen elsewhere in the Mediterranean. Dusky groupers hang off the wall while conger eels, scorpionfish and spiny lobsters wedge into the cracks. Diving here is permitted only with a licensed centre inside Kornati National Park.

conditionsByMonth.suitRecommendation: 7mm wetsuit with hood; cooler below the thermocline
7mm wetsuit with hood; cooler below the thermocline

getThere: Fly into Zadar (ZAD) or Split (SPU), both served by seasonal European flights. From either, reach the harbour town of Murter, the main gateway to the park, and join a licensed dive boat for the crossing of roughly 19 nautical miles to the northern Kornati islands. Day boats and liveaboards also run from Zadar and Biograd.
notes: Diving inside Kornati National Park is allowed only through a licensed dive centre, in designated zones, and a daily park ticket is required. The richest gorgonian growth sits below 25 metres, so plan for cold water at depth and conservative no decompression limits.

name: Chandelier Cave
description: A flooded limestone sea cave in Malakal Harbor, a few minutes by boat from Koror, where five chambers run back into the rock and four of them trap pockets of breathable air. Divers drop through the entrance at about 4 m, follow the divemaster through shallow submerged passages, and surface inside the chambers to stand among stalactites and stalagmites that took tens of thousands of years to grow, fingers of rock hanging from the ceiling to meet columns rising off the floor. Depth stays under 15 m and the water is still, but the chambers are dark and silt clouds easily, so a torch and slow, controlled buoyancy matter. Out at the entrance wall, cardinalfish and soldierfish gather in the shadows, banded coral shrimp work the cracks, and mandarinfish appear around dusk.
getThere: Fly into Koror (ROR / Roman Tmetuchl International), Palau's only international airport, with connections from Manila, Taipei, Guam, and Tokyo. The cave sits in Malakal Harbor on the south side of Koror, a five to ten minute boat ride from town dive shops, so it is usually run as a second or third dive of the day rather than a dedicated trip.

siteSpecificGear.name: Primary dive light
siteSpecificGear.reason: The inner chambers are an overhead environment with little natural light, so a torch is needed to see the stalactite formations and the way back out.

siteSpecificGear.name: Backup light
siteSpecificGear.reason: Standard redundancy for the overhead sections in case the primary torch floods or fails.

notes: Overhead environment: stay with the guide, carry a torch, and move slowly because the fine sediment clouds the chambers fast and the formations are fragile. No technical cave certification is required and depth stays shallow, but it suits divers comfortable with buoyancy. Sheltered harbor location means it dives year round regardless of swell. Requires the Koror State permit and Palau Pristine Paradise Environmental Fee. Often paired with a dusk mandarinfish dive on the nearby Malakal Harbor wall.

name: Japanese Gardens
description: A drift dive off the southern tip of Goat Island, where the Guyana Current pushes divers along a slope crowded with orange elephant ear sponges, yellow tube sponges and grey barrel sponges before funneling them through the Kamikaze Cut, a narrow gap that speeds up the flow. The same nutrient laden water that grows those sponges feeds hawksbill turtles, nurse sharks tucked under ledges, and schools of barracuda and tarpon, with manta rays passing through in the greener plankton months. The dive runs from a sponge covered shelf near the island down past 30 m.

Bottom-dwelling, largely nocturnal sharks that spend much of the day resting in groups under coral ledges or on sandy substrate. Nurse sharks are identifiable by their broad, flattened heads, small eyes, and twin nasal barbels used to sense prey in sand and rubble. They feed on crustaceans, molluscs, and small fish, using powerful suction to extract prey from crevices. Among the least threatening sharks to divers — slow-moving, benign, and tolerant of close approach when resting. They should not be handled; bites from provoked individuals, while rare, are powerful.

getThere: Fly into A.N.R. Robinson International (TAB) at Crown Point in southwest Tobago, with frequent hops from Port of Spain on Trinidad and seasonal service from the UK and North America. Speyside sits on the northeast coast about 50 km away, a drive of roughly 1.5 hours along the windward coast road. Dive operators in Speyside Bay run boats to the south tip of Goat Island in about 10 minutes.
notes: Strong drift is both the draw and the hazard: the current accelerates through a gap the guides call the Kamikaze Cut, so expect a fast ride and carry an SMB for the live boat pickup. It dives best on a slack to building tide with a guide who knows the timing. Plankton heavy water from the Guyana Current keeps visibility variable and feeds the sponges. The site lies within northeast Tobago waters managed for reef protection, so spearfishing and glove use are discouraged.

name: Barren Island
description: India's only active volcano breaks the surface about 140 km northeast of Port Blair, and the reef ringing its base is unlike anywhere else in the Andamans — the sand here is black volcanic ash, not white, and old lava flows have set into stepped ledges, arches and walls that drop past 100 m. Reef manta rays are the headline: a group of up to nine works the cleaning stations off the western black sand bay, banking slowly while cleaner wrasse pick them over. Whitetip reef sharks patrol the drop offs, green and hawksbill turtles graze the shallows, and schools of needlefish, barracuda and trevally hang in water that routinely clears to 40 m or more. Sites such as the Washing Machine throw strong down currents, and with the island reachable only by liveaboard this stays firmly advanced ground.

Barren Island lies about 140 km northeast of Port Blair and roughly 100 km from Havelock (Swaraj Dweep), with no jetty and no permitted landing, so it is reached only by liveaboard or a long private dive charter. The open ocean crossing runs about 4 to 5 hours from Port Blair or 2 to 3 hours from Havelock, and most divers join an organised multi day expedition rather than a day boat.

siteSpecificGear.name: Dive light or torch
siteSpecificGear.reason: Lava ledges, arches and the deeper walls fall into shadow, and a primary torch brings out the colour of the gorgonian fans and helps with shark and turtle ID.

siteSpecificGear.name: Nitrox cert + EAN32 fills
siteSpecificGear.reason: Manta cleaning stations and the lava reef sit deep enough that air bottom time is short; EAN32 stretches no deco limits and is worth arranging with the liveaboard before departure.

notes: Advanced Open Water with solid current experience is the working minimum; sites like the Washing Machine throw strong down currents. Landing on Barren Island is prohibited, it is an active volcano (last erupted 2017 to 2018) and a protected zone, so all diving is from boats with no shore access. The season runs roughly October to May; the southwest monsoon from June to September makes the offshore crossing unsafe. Trips run by liveaboard and book out well ahead because few vessels are permitted here. Keep clear of mantas on the cleaning stations and do not touch the gorgonian fans.

name: First Cathedral
description: A collapsed volcanic lava tube off Lanai's leeward south coast, southeast of Manele Bay, forms a cavern the size of a small chapel: roughly 30 m long and two stories tall, entered through a wide archway whose floor drops to about 18 m. Where the roof caved in, holes in the ceiling let shafts of sunlight pour onto a fallen block of basalt that divers call the Altar, and on calm summer middays the beams turn the chamber into a stained glass effect that gave the site its name. Walls crusted with orange cup coral shelter green sea turtles, resting whitetip reef sharks, spiny lobster wedged into cracks and clouds of endemic Hawaiian reef fish. The classic finish is the Shotgun, a narrow chimney at the back of the cavern where divers time the surge and get flushed into open water one at a time.

species.ecologicalDescription: A large, air-breathing reptile that returns to the same nesting beaches generation after generation. Divers encounter green sea turtles resting under coral ledges, cruising reef edges, or feeding on algae and seagrass. They are often habituated to slow-moving divers at popular sites. Their slow growth rate — taking 20–50 years to reach sexual maturity — means that even small levels of adult mortality have outsized population impacts. Endangered globally but recovering in regions with strong nesting beach protection.

A slender, nocturnal predator instantly identified by the white tips on its dorsal and caudal fins. During the day, whitetips rest motionless in groups on sandy ledges or inside reef caves — divers frequently swim directly over resting aggregations. At night they become highly active hunters, pursuing fish and octopus through reef crevices with remarkable agility. Unlike many sharks, they are non-territorial toward divers and typically ignore human presence. Listed as vulnerable; their slow reproductive rate makes populations sensitive to fishing pressure.

getThere: Fly into Kahului Airport (OGG) on Maui. First Cathedral is dived almost entirely from Maui: charter boats leave Lahaina and Maalaea harbors and cross the Auau Channel to Lanai's sheltered south coast in about an hour, with the calmest water on early morning departures. A few operators run from Manele Harbor on Lanai, reached by the Expeditions passenger ferry from Lahaina. The site sits in Maui County, not on the Kona Coast of the Big Island.
notes: This is a cavern dive in an overhead environment, entered through an archway and finished through a tight chimney called the Shotgun where divers ride the surge out one at a time, so most operators require Advanced Open Water or a confident certified diver with good buoyancy. Sand stirred off the floor clouds the chamber fast, so the first group in gets the cleanest light, and the sunbeams on the Altar are sharpest on calm summer middays near noon. Winter Kona storms and rougher channel crossings cancel trips at short notice.

name: Paradise Reef
description: Paradise Reef is the shallow coral strip just south of Cozumel's cruise piers and the northernmost reef inside the island's national marine park. Three low ridges of sponges and gorgonians sit in 9 to 15 m of gentle drift, which makes it the standard Cozumel checkout dive and its most reliable night dive. After dark, torch beams pick out the splendid toadfish, a striped electric blue fish that lives nowhere on Earth but Cozumel, wedged under ledges and croaking from its burrow. Spotted eagle rays pass through in winter while octopus, banded coral shrimp and snapper work the reef once the sun drops.

species.ecologicalDescription: Elegant, wing-shaped rays recognised by a white-spotted black dorsum and a long, whip-like tail. Spotted eagle rays are active swimmers, covering large distances in open water and occasionally forming large feeding schools. They prey on buried molluscs and crustaceans, using their flat, plate-like teeth to crush shells. Often encountered cruising along reef edges or in blue water above the reef. Near threatened globally; highly susceptible to bycatch. A highlight of any dive — their wing-beat motion in open water is one of the ocean's most graceful sights.

getThere: Cozumel (CZM) has direct flights from many US cities, or fly into Cancun (CUN) and take the 45 minute ferry from Playa del Carmen. Paradise Reef is a few minutes by boat from the San Miguel waterfront, just south of the cruise terminals.

siteSpecificGear.name: Primary dive torch
siteSpecificGear.reason: Paradise is dived mainly after dark, when a strong torch is what reveals the splendid toadfish under ledges.

siteSpecificGear.name: Surface marker buoy
siteSpecificGear.reason: The reef sits beside the cruise ship channel, so divers surface under an SMB clear of boat traffic.

notes: Inside Cozumel Reefs National Park, so a park fee or wristband applies. The site borders the cruise ship channel and dives are timed around heavy boat traffic. Night dives are the highlight.

name: Shark Ray Alley
description: Zone D of Hol Chan Marine Reserve, about a mile south of the reserve's main cut off Ambergris Caye. Decades of fish cleaning by local fishermen drew Atlantic nurse sharks and southern stingrays into the shallow sand patch, and now twenty or more sharks routinely circle in waist deep water as boats arrive. Depths run only 5 to 12 feet over a white sand bottom, so divers and snorkelers share the column with the animals. The draw is close encounters and natural light photography rather than reef structure, and most operators pair it with a Hol Chan reef dive on the same trip.

species.ecologicalDescription: A solitary apex predator with a reputation exceeding its actual threat to divers. Great barracuda are ambush hunters, hovering motionless in mid-water before striking fish at high speed using rows of razor-sharp teeth. Their habit of following divers — likely investigating the reflection and movement of equipment — can feel intimidating but is almost always investigative rather than aggressive. They reach up to 1.8 metres. Flesh can carry ciguatera toxin in tropical regions; recreational encounters are considered low risk.

A large, air-breathing reptile that returns to the same nesting beaches generation after generation. Divers encounter green sea turtles resting under coral ledges, cruising reef edges, or feeding on algae and seagrass. They are often habituated to slow-moving divers at popular sites. Their slow growth rate — taking 20–50 years to reach sexual maturity — means that even small levels of adult mortality have outsized population impacts. Endangered globally but recovering in regions with strong nesting beach protection.

getThere: Fly into Philip S. W. Goldson International Airport (BZE) near Belize City, then take a 15 minute Tropic Air or Maya Island Air hop to San Pedro on Ambergris Caye (SPR). Most San Pedro dive operators run the trip as a half day boat charter combined with Hol Chan, roughly 20 minutes south of town.

lodging.label: Victoria House Resort & Spa Ambergris Caye

operators.label: Amigos del Mar – Shark Ray Alley

notes: Inside Hol Chan Marine Reserve (Zone D), so a per person park fee applies and is usually bundled by operators. No gloves, no touching, no chasing. Sharks are habituated and generally calm but bites have occurred when divers grab them or get between them and bait. Often combined with a Hol Chan reef dive on the same boat trip. Suitable as a snorkel or for first dives; current is typically mild.

name: Aida II Wreck
description: A 75 m steel supply ship that struck Big Brother in storm winds on 15 September 1957 while offloading personnel for the island lighthouse. The hull broke in two: the engine block lies wedged on the reef at 7 m where the surf caught her, the bow rests against the wall at 30 m, the deck and railings run down past 50 m, and the propeller sits at 65 m for tech divers only. Soft corals and gorgonians now sheath every steel rib, clouds of glassfish boil through the holds, and grey reef sharks cruise the blue off her stern. She lies a few hundred metres along the same north reef as the Numidia and is almost always run as the second dive of the day.

species.ecologicalDescription: One of the Indo-Pacific's most abundant reef sharks and a defining presence on healthy coral reefs. Grey reef sharks are mid-water patrollers, typically seen in small groups or alone along reef edges and drop-offs. They are curious rather than aggressive, often circling divers at a consistent distance. A distinctive threat display — arched back, depressed pectoral fins, exaggerated swimming — signals discomfort if divers approach too closely. Near threatened; their numbers have declined sharply in areas with intensive fishing.

Among the largest bony fish on coral reefs, male Napoleon wrasse (also called humphead wrasse) can reach 2 metres and are unmistakable: a steep forehead hump, thick fleshy lips, and vivid blue-green patterning. They feed on hard-shelled invertebrates including sea urchins and crown-of-thorns starfish, playing an important regulatory role on reefs. Solitary and slow-moving, they are often habituated to divers at popular sites. Endangered globally due to targeted fishing for the live reef food fish trade.

One of the ocean's most visually striking reptiles, recognisable by its narrow, pointed beak and richly patterned shell. Hawksbills feed primarily on sponges, making them a keystone species on coral reefs — their grazing prevents sponges from overgrowing and smothering coral. Divers most often encounter them resting under coral ledges or methodically picking at reef walls. Critically endangered due to historical shell trade and ongoing egg harvesting, global populations have partially recovered in protected areas. Their presence is a strong indicator of a healthy, structurally complex reef.

getThere: Liveaboard only, departing Hurghada (HRG) or Marsa Alam (RMF) with direct European flights. Southern Red Sea itineraries taking in Brothers, Daedalus and Elphinstone run 5 to 7 nights and reach the El Ikhwa (Brother) Islands offshore in the central Red Sea.

lodging.label: Emperor Elite – Red Sea Brothers Itinerary

notes: Brothers Marine Park is liveaboard only and generally accessible from March to October. The Aida descends a near vertical wall: engine block at 7 m, bow at 30 m, midship past 50 m and propeller at 65 m, so the lower hull is technical or trimix only. Strong, unpredictable currents off the point demand reef hooks and SMBs.

name: Nudi Falls (Lembeh Strait)
description: Mainland side mark in the middle of the Lembeh Strait, just north of Tandu Rusa village. The dive starts shallow on a soft coral encrusted wall that drops to about 15 m, then transitions to a rubble and sand slope feeding a broad field of large soft corals from 20 m down. The site earned its name because divers' exhaust bubbles dislodge nudibranchs from the wall above, sending tiny slugs raining down through the water column. It is also the most reliable spot in the strait for the Lembeh seadragon, Pontoh's pygmy seahorse, harlequin shrimp, rhinopias scorpionfish, wonderpus and blue ringed octopus, and ornate ghost pipefish. Currents are typically calm.
getThere: Fly into Sam Ratulangi International (MDC) in Manado, North Sulawesi. From the airport it is a 90 minute road transfer to Bitung port, then a short crossing by traditional outrigger or resort speedboat to one of the Lembeh resorts. Nudi Falls sits in the middle of the strait on the mainland side, roughly a 10 minute boat ride from most resort jetties.
notes: Classic muck and critter site. Bring a focus light, a pointer, and a macro lens (60 to 105 mm). Buoyancy discipline is essential: the sand below the wall holds seadragons and pygmy pipehorses that one careless fin kick can bury. The wall itself is decorated with delicate soft corals and crinoids that should never be touched. Best diving in dry season (March through October) when visibility improves, though macro life is rich year round.

name: Cara a Cara
description: Roatan's signature shark dive on a 21 m sand plateau off the south coast near Cordelia Banks. A resident group of 10 to 15 Caribbean reef sharks, almost all mature females reaching 2 to 3 m, circles a baited drum while divers kneel in a half ring on the sand. The reef edge drops off behind the action and the closing passes bring the animals within arm's length. Current can rip across the plateau between sets.

species.ecologicalDescription: The dominant large shark on Caribbean coral reefs, characterised by a stocky build and rounded snout. Caribbean reef sharks patrol reef edges and drop-offs, often in loose groups, and are the species most commonly encountered in Caribbean shark dives. They are opportunistic predators of fish and cephalopods, and play a critical top-down regulatory role on the reef. Near threatened; heavily fished for fins and meat across their range. At sites with dive tourism value, local protection has allowed populations to partially recover.

Great barracuda are ambush hunters, hovering motionless in mid-water before striking fish at high speed using rows of razor-sharp teeth. They reach up to 1.8 metres. Flesh can carry ciguatera toxin in tropical regions; recreational encounters are considered low risk.

getThere: Fly into Roatan (RTB / Juan Manuel Galvez International) which has direct flights from several US hubs plus connections via San Pedro Sula (SAP). The dive runs as a half day boat trip out of West End, West Bay, or French Cay marinas; expect 25 to 35 minutes of transit each way.

siteSpecificGear.name: Reef hook
siteSpecificGear.reason: Current can push divers off the sand circle between bait passes; a hook lets you hold position without scraping the bottom.

notes: Baited shark dive run under a permitted operator. Divers stay in a stationary semicircle on the sand at 21 m while staff present a bait drum; do not chase the animals. The sharks are habituated and have produced no recorded recreational fatalities, but a baited environment is not without risk. Advanced certification and a recent dive log are typically required.

name: Steve's Bommie
description: An isolated coral tower on Ribbon Reef Number 3 that climbs from a 30 m sand floor to within 5 m of the surface. Schools of bigeye trevally, fusiliers and yellow lined snapper rotate around the pinnacle in dense columns while macro hunters search the crevices for leafy scorpionfish, stonefish, longnose hawkfish and peacock mantis shrimp. Anemonefish defend host anemones near the summit and grey, whitetip and blacktip reef sharks patrol the deeper edges. A memorial plaque to Steve, the free diver the site is named after, sits near the base at about 25 m.

species.ecologicalDescription: Schooling predators that form dense, swirling baitballs during the day at cleaning stations and reef edges — one of the most photogenic spectacles on Indo-Pacific reefs. The school rotates slowly, each fish orienting toward the current, creating a living silver cylinder that opens and closes around divers. At dusk, the school disperses and individuals hunt cooperatively across the reef flat. Their large eyes are adapted for low-light feeding. Bigeye trevally are important prey for large sharks and groupers, connecting mid-water and reef food webs.

During the day, whitetips rest motionless in groups on sandy ledges or inside reef caves — divers frequently swim directly over resting aggregations. At night they become highly active hunters, pursuing fish and octopus through reef crevices with remarkable agility.
