Common lionfish hover in the shaded overhangs and swim-through entrances of Cathedral Rock, their elaborate venomous spines fanned outward in a warning display that is nonetheless more defensive than offensive. They are most active at dusk when they begin herding small fish into corners using their broad pectoral fins before striking, and night dives at Cathedral Rock reveal their hunting behavior in full. The rock's complex architecture provides the sheltered daytime refuges this species prefers.

getThere: Cathedral Rock is a 10 to 20 minute banca ride from the main Anilao and Mabini dive resort cluster. It is accessible to Open Water divers in calm conditions and is a standard inclusion on multi-site day trips.

name: Buccoo Reef
description: Buccoo Reef is Trinidad and Tobago's most celebrated coral lagoon, a shallow protected system where brain and staghorn corals form dense gardens patrolled by hawksbill turtles and green morays. The calm, clear lagoon interior shelters juvenile fish in huge numbers — snapper, grunt, and French angelfish move through in loose shoals while nurse sharks rest in sandy pockets beneath coral heads. Because of its marine park status the reef shows genuine recovery, with coral cover noticeably healthier than many Caribbean counterparts.

species.ecologicalDescription: Hawksbill turtles are resident foragers at Buccoo, feeding on sponges and sea fans within the protected lagoon. Their presence year-round reflects the reef's healthy sponge communities, which form a critical part of their diet. Encounters at shallow depths make these among the most accessible turtle dives in the southern Caribbean.

Nurse sharks rest in groups beneath coral overhangs and in sandy channels throughout Buccoo's lagoon system. As benthic predators they keep invertebrate populations in check, and their docile nature makes them iconic subjects for divers. Multiple individuals are often seen on a single dive, a sign of a reef with intact elasmobrach communities.

French angelfish are abundant throughout the staghorn and brain coral formations, grazing on sponges and algae that would otherwise smother coral. They often move in mated pairs, territorial and bold, making close-up photography straightforward. Their prevalence is a reliable indicator of a reef in good ecological condition.

getThere: Access from Tobago's Buccoo village via boat; most operators are based in Crown Point or Scarborough on Tobago.

name: Caroni Mangrove Dive
description: The Caroni Swamp on Trinidad's west coast is one of the Caribbean's most unusual dive environments — a nutrient-rich mangrove estuary where visibility is low but the biomass is extraordinary, with tarpon rolling in silver clouds and snook hanging motionless beneath prop roots. The Orinoco outflow enriches these waters with plankton, drawing baitfish and the predators that follow them into a genuinely wilderness setting accessible by boat from Port of Spain. This is macro and wide-angle photography at its most atmospheric, where shafts of filtered green light illuminate mangrove roots encrusted with oysters, sea squirts, and juvenile reef fish.

species.ecologicalDescription: Tarpon gather in the Caroni mangroves in large schools, using the sheltered estuary as a feeding ground and transitional zone between open sea and freshwater tributaries. As apex predators in the estuary they regulate the dense baitfish populations that thrive on the plankton-rich Orinoco outflow. Encounters with rolling 1.5-meter tarpon in shallow mangrove channels are among the most memorable in Caribbean diving.

Snook are ambush predators perfectly suited to the dim mangrove channels, hovering mid-water or beneath overhangs waiting for prey to pass. They are highly sensitive to salinity gradients and their concentration in the Caroni reflects the estuary's mix of fresh and salt water, which produces the invertebrate diversity they depend on. Snook are a priority species for local conservation since they are heavily fished in open water but protected within Caroni Swamp.

A small population of American crocodiles inhabits the deeper channels of Caroni Swamp, making this one of very few dive sites where crocodilian encounters are genuinely possible. They are shy and primarily nocturnal, and sightings are rare but documented — typically resting on muddy banks or submerged at channel edges. Their presence is an indicator of exceptional ecosystem health in the swamp.

getThere: Boat access from the Caroni Bird Sanctuary landing, roughly 20 minutes south of Port of Spain on Trinidad's west coast. Very few operators offer this dive — arrange in advance.

name: Chagville Point
description: Chagville Point on Trinidad's northwest peninsula is the island's premier open-water reef dive, where a rocky headland drops to a rubble slope at 25 meters hosting nurse sharks, spotted eagle rays, and occasional southern stingrays. The point catches upwelling from the Columbus Channel which brings nutrients and good visibility on outgoing tides, and the hard coral communities here are less affected by Orinoco sediment than sites further south. Mornings see eagle rays cruising the slope in pairs while yellowfin goatfish root through the rubble below.

species.ecologicalDescription: Spotted eagle rays are the signature species at Chagville Point, drawn by the mollusks and crustaceans buried in the rubble slope. They typically travel in pairs or small groups, their distinctive white-spotted mantles visible from 15 meters away as they glide past the reef edge. The Columbus Channel upwelling concentrates their prey, making this one of the most reliable eagle ray sites in Trinidad.

Nurse sharks rest in small aggregations under the ledges along the base of Chagville's reef slope, often three or four animals together in a single overhang. They are nocturnal hunters of lobster and small fish but are reliably encountered at rest during daytime dives. Their aggregation behavior at this site suggests long-term site fidelity and an undisturbed population.

Dense schools of yellowfin goatfish work the rubble margins below the reef slope, using chemosensory barbels to detect buried worms and crustaceans. They serve as a key prey species for the eagle rays and nurse sharks that make this site famous, and their abundance indicates a productive, nutrient-rich benthic environment. Schools of 200 or more individuals are common in the 10 to 20 meter range.

getThere: Boat from Chagville Beach on Trinidad's northwest peninsula, approximately 45 minutes by road from Port of Spain then a short boat ride to the point.

name: Gasparee Island Caves
description: Gasparee Island in the Gulf of Paria contains an extraordinary network of underwater limestone caves and caverns, with stalactite-lined chambers descending to 20 meters and opening into cenote-like pools illuminated by shafts of blue light from surface openings. The caves shelter dense colonies of glass shrimp and cave-dwelling fish including cardinalfish and bigeyes, while the walls are draped in encrusting sponges in brilliant orange and red. The site is unique in the southern Caribbean — its mix of geological spectacle and macro life rivals the famous cenotes of Mexico at a fraction of the visitor numbers.

species.ecologicalDescription: Glasseye snappers pack into the cave overhangs in tight schools, using low-light zones to avoid predation during daytime while feeding on invertebrates at night. Their large eyes are an adaptation to the dim cave environment, and dense aggregations of 50 or more individuals hovering in beam light are a hallmark experience at Gasparee. They are a key link between the cave ecosystem and the open reef, carrying nutrients out of the cave when they disperse at dusk.

The cave walls at Gasparee support spectacular growths of orange and red encrusting sponges, which thrive in the low-light, high-current cave entrances. These sponges filter enormous volumes of water and provide structural habitat for the shrimp and small fish that colonize the cave walls. Their presence indicates excellent water quality in the Gulf of Paria micro-environment around the island.

Pederson cleaner shrimp establish cleaning stations at the cave mouth and in shallow cavern sections, waving their antennae to attract passing fish. They remove parasites and dead tissue from fish clients including moray eels and grouper, providing a service that maintains reef fish health. Their abundance at Gasparee reflects the mix of open-reef fish visiting the caves and the protected substrate the caves offer.

getThere: Boat from Carenage or Chaguaramas on Trinidad's northwest peninsula; Gasparee Island is a short 15 minute crossing from the Chaguaramas marina.

name: Isla Los Testigos Reef
description: The main reef system wrapping the largest island of Los Testigos is an almost completely undisturbed Caribbean reef ecosystem, where coral cover exceeds 60 percent and staghorn thickets shelter enormous populations of parrotfish, surgeonfish, and snapper that have never experienced fishing pressure. The reef terrace runs from 5 to 22 meters before dropping into deeper blue, and the clarity of the water — often exceeding 35 meters horizontal visibility — allows wide-angle photography that captures the full scale of pristine reef architecture. Whale sharks pass through seasonally between December and April, feeding in the plankton-rich surface waters around the island group.

species.ecologicalDescription: Whale sharks pass through Los Testigos waters between December and April, drawn by the seasonal plankton blooms that develop in the upwelling-influenced waters of the southeastern Caribbean. Encounters typically occur at the surface or in the top 20 meters where filter feeding is most productive, and the remote location means sightings are uncontested with boats. Individual identification by spot patterns is possible, and sightings here may represent a previously undocumented seasonal aggregation.

Princess parrotfish are abundant across the reef terrace, grazing on algae-encrusted coral rubble and producing the white sand that forms Los Testigos's beaches. Their populations are unusually dense compared to fished Caribbean reefs, reflecting the near-total absence of human exploitation at this remote site. Supermale individuals in vivid green and pink terminal phase are particularly conspicuous on the shallow reef flat.

Bar jacks form large polarized schools over the reef edge at Los Testigos, hunting cooperatively to herd baitfish against the reef structure. Their metallic blue-silver flanks with the characteristic black and electric-blue lateral stripe flash as schools wheel in unison — a sight amplified by the exceptional visibility. These schools reach several hundred individuals at Los Testigos, a population size that indicates an unfished, fully functioning reef ecosystem.

getThere: Liveaboard from Margarita Island (Porlamar) is the primary access — Los Testigos lies approximately 100km northeast and has no permanent dive infrastructure. Day trips exist but are rare.

name: Punta Sur Wall
description: The southern tip of Los Testigos drops into a sheer vertical wall beginning at 12 meters and descending beyond recreational limits, draped in enormous black coral trees, sea fans, and barrel sponges that took centuries to reach their current size. A light to moderate current sweeps the wall face, delivering nutrients that feed dense invertebrate communities and attracting schooling Atlantic spadefish, creole wrasse, and large amberjack that hang off the wall edge in glittering masses. This is the most dramatic topography in the archipelago, combining the visual scale of a deep wall with the life density of an untouched Caribbean reef.

species.ecologicalDescription: Black coral trees at Punta Sur wall reach heights of 2 meters or more, representing colonies several hundred years old in an ecosystem that has never experienced collection pressure. They provide critical structural habitat for hawkfish, shrimp, and juvenile fish that shelter in their branches. The density and size of black coral colonies here is a direct indicator of how rarely this wall has been visited — harvested reefs elsewhere in the Caribbean have lost 90 percent or more of their black coral.

Atlantic spadefish aggregate in large schools off the lip of the Punta Sur wall, their striking black-and-silver barring visible against the blue water column as they face into the current. Schools of 100 to 300 individuals are common at this site, feeding on jellyfish and zooplankton carried past the wall by the prevailing southeasterly current. Spadefish aggregations of this size are rarely seen at Caribbean dive sites where even light fishing pressure has depleted them.

Greater amberjack patrol the wall edge at Punta Sur in groups of 5 to 15 individuals, using the current as cover to approach smaller reef fish. At Los Testigos they show little fear of divers and will approach closely out of curiosity before resuming their patrol — behavior characteristic of populations with no experience of spearfishing. Their presence confirms the functioning pelagic-reef link that characterizes remote, fully protected reef systems.

getThere: Liveaboard from Margarita Island; Punta Sur is reached by approximately 20 minutes of boat travel from the main island anchorage within the archipelago.

name: El Banco Seamount
description: El Banco is an underwater seamount rising to 18 meters below the surface several kilometers northeast of the main Los Testigos island group, a submarine pinnacle that concentrates hammerhead sharks, silky sharks, and enormous schools of horse-eye jacks in conditions that rival Socorro and Cocos for pelagic intensity without the crowds. The seamount top is encrusted with gorgonian sea fans and acts as a cleaning station — hammerheads queue along the upcurrent face while bluestriped grunt and creole wrasse hover in attendance. In December through April the same whale sharks that visit the main reef also circle the seamount, sometimes for extended periods.

species.ecologicalDescription: Scalloped hammerheads visit El Banco seamount in groups of 10 to 40 individuals, circling the upcurrent face at depths between 20 and 35 meters where the cleaning station activity is concentrated. They are more reliably encountered during the dry season months of December through April when cooler, cleaner water increases visibility and concentrates prey around the seamount. Their presence at this remote seamount underscores the ecological importance of the Los Testigos submarine plateau as a pelagic aggregation point.

Horse-eye jacks form massive tornado schools above El Banco seamount, sometimes reaching several thousand individuals that form a swirling silver column above the pinnacle. As midwater predators they respond to both schooling baitfish concentrated by the seamount topography and to the upwelling currents that bring nutrients from depth. Descending into the center of a horse-eye jack tornado is one of the defining experiences at El Banco.

Silky sharks are the most consistently present large shark at El Banco, circling the seamount at mid-water depths and occasionally diving to the summit. They are oceanic sharks that use seamounts as navigational waypoints and feeding aggregation zones, and their year-round presence at Los Testigos suggests the seamount lies on a regular circuit for local individuals. At this unvisited site they approach closely, exhibiting investigative behavior rarely seen where sharks have been conditioned to avoid boats.

getThere: Liveaboard from Margarita Island; El Banco requires navigating open water northeast of the island group and is only accessible in calm conditions — best attempted on liveaboard itineraries that allow flexible scheduling.

name: North Channel
description: The North Channel cuts between two of the Los Testigos islands, funneling current through a narrow gap where reef walls on both sides are packed with sea fans, tube sponges, and barrel sponges reaching 1.5 meters in height, while the channel floor is an extraordinary carpet of soft corals in purple and yellow. The current through the channel attracts schooling barracuda — hundreds at a time forming the characteristic cylindrical tornado of the great barracuda — along with green moray eels hunting the rubble margins and eagle rays gliding past in pairs. Slack water periods allow exploratory drifting along the walls while stronger flow concentrates all the action at the channel mouth in a genuinely dramatic spectacle.

species.ecologicalDescription: Great barracuda aggregate in the North Channel in schooling tornados of 200 to 500 individuals, a behavior typical of currents that concentrate baitfish and trigger cooperative herding. The channel's channelized flow creates the precise hydrodynamic conditions that barracuda exploit to minimize swimming effort while maximizing foraging opportunity. Tornados typically form at mid-water in 15 to 20 meters, slowly rotating as individual fish cycle through the school.

Green morays of exceptional size inhabit the rubble and coral base of the North Channel walls, some individuals reaching 2 meters or more in a habitat with no predation pressure from fishing. They hunt actively during current-assisted tides and rest in crevices during slack periods, their olive-green mucus coating giving them a distinctive color against the orange sponge walls. Multiple morays sharing the same boulder cluster suggest a high-density, food-rich environment typical of undisturbed reef systems.

Queen angelfish are conspicuous throughout the North Channel walls, their electric blue and yellow flanks making them among the most visually striking reef fish in the Caribbean. At Los Testigos they are unusually bold, feeding on sponges in open water rather than retreating to coral crevices as they do on heavily visited reefs. Mated pairs defend sponge-feeding territories along the channel walls, and the density of individuals reflects an intact, sponge-rich reef community.

getThere: Liveaboard from Margarita Island; the North Channel is accessible by dinghy from a liveaboard anchored in the main island group lagoon, with entry timed to current cycles.

name: Bida Nok
description: The larger of the two uninhabited Bida islets south of Phi Phi Le. A near-vertical wall on the west side drops from 3 m to beyond 30 m, encrusted with sea fans, barrel sponges, and black coral. Leopard sharks park on the sandy ledges at 18 to 22 m throughout the year. Strong upwellings on the southwest corner attract bumphead parrotfish and occasional whale sharks during the March to April window.
getThere: Speedboat from Phi Phi Don (Tonsai pier) takes 15 minutes. Day trip boats from Phuket or Krabi run directly to Bida Nok. No mooring at the islet itself — dive boats use their own anchors or drift anchoring.

name: Bida Nai
description: The smaller of the twin Bida islets, with a shallower reef profile that makes it ideal for less experienced divers and night dives. Hard coral coverage on the north face is exceptional — fields of staghorn and brain coral that survived the 2010 bleaching event better than most Andaman sites. Titan triggerfish are territorial in the shallows; blue-spotted stingrays cruise the sandy channels between coral heads.
getThere: 15-minute speedboat ride from Tonsai pier on Phi Phi Don. Night dive trips depart around 18:00 from Phi Phi Don; book through any dive shop on the island. Day trip boats from Phuket or Krabi combine Bida Nai with Bida Nok.

name: Shark Point (Hin Bida)
description: Three submerged pinnacles between Phi Phi and the mainland are among the most celebrated dive sites in the Andaman Sea. Encrusted in purple soft coral and sea anemones, the tops of the pinnacles sit at 18 m. Currents funnel past and bring leopard sharks — often six or more resting side by side on the flat sand — and passing mantis shrimp colonies in the rubble. A UNESCO-listed marine sanctuary zone since 1981.
getThere: 45-minute speedboat from Phi Phi Don or 90 minutes from Phuket's Chalong Bay. Dive shops on Phi Phi Don run dedicated morning trips. The site is inside the Hat Noppharat Thara Mu Ko Phi Phi National Park; a park entry fee applies.

name: Maya Bay Pinnacle
description: An underwater pinnacle rising from 28 m to within 8 m of the surface just outside the famous Maya Bay lagoon on Phi Phi Le. While the beach above was closed for rehabilitation from 2018 to 2022, the reef recovered visibly. Schools of chevron barracuda orbit the pinnacle top, and the sloping walls are busy with sergeant majors, anthias, and butterflyfish. Occasional leopard shark sightings on the sandy floor below 22 m.
getThere: 15-minute speedboat from Phi Phi Don's Tonsai pier to the south end of Phi Phi Le. National park entry fee required. Dive trips combine this site with Bida Nok or Bida Nai on the same day.

name: Stonehenge
description: A forest of granite boulders arranged in stacked formations on the southwest side of Koh Lipe, dropping from 5 m to 28 m. The boulders are draped in soft corals and encrusting sponges; cracks and crevices shelter moray eels, lionfish, and sleeping nurse sharks. Currents funnel between the boulders during mid-tide, drawing schooling barracuda and trevally. One of the most photogenic dive sites in Tarutao National Marine Park.
getThere: 10-minute longtail boat from Koh Lipe's Sunrise Beach or Pattaya Beach. All dive shops on Lipe run morning and afternoon trips. The site is within Tarutao National Marine Park; a park fee is collected at the pier.

name: Koh Usen
description: A small uninhabited island 3 km southwest of Lipe with a submerged ridge running off its northern tip into open water. The ridge top at 12 m has some of the best tabletop acropora in the park; beyond it the bottom slopes to 30 m and terminates in a sandy plain used as a resting area by green and hawksbill turtles. Bumphead parrotfish visit in aggregations of up to 30 individuals during the early morning flood tide between November and February.
getThere: 20-minute speedboat from Koh Lipe. Dive operators run early morning departures to catch the bumphead parrotfish aggregation at first light during high season. The crossing is exposed to open sea swell — trips may be cancelled during southwest monsoon.

name: Eight Mile Rock
description: A solitary seamount eight nautical miles southwest of Lipe, rising from 40 m to within 12 m of the surface. This is Lipe's premier big-animal site: manta rays are sighted here reliably from December to March, whale sharks pass through January to April, and schools of hammerhead sharks have been recorded on the deeper flanks. Strong and unpredictable currents make this an advanced dive; the reward is blue water pelagic action above a hard coral cap in outstanding health.
getThere: 35-minute speedboat from Koh Lipe. Advanced divers only — strong current experience required. Dive operators recommend a DSMB for every diver. Trips run weather-permitting from November through April only; the site is inaccessible during southwest monsoon.

name: Hin Ngam
description: A shallow reef plateau extending north of Hin Ngam island, a tiny islet famous on the surface for its smooth, colourful pebbles. Underwater, the gently sloping reef from 3 m to 18 m is blanketed in diverse hard coral, making it one of the best entry-level sites in the park. Clownfish in anemones are abundant across the shallow top; the deeper rubble margin hosts flatheads, cuttlefish, and a reliable resident blue-ringed octopus population.
getThere: 15-minute longtail boat from Koh Lipe's Sunrise Beach. The shallow depth and calm conditions in the north make this suitable for first dives and snorkelling. Night dive trips depart from Lipe around 18:30 and are run by several operators on the island.

name: Shark Point
description: One of the signature dives of the Gili Islands, Shark Point sits off the southern tip of Gili Trawangan where the reef shelf drops sharply into open water. Blacktip reef sharks cruise the upper slope at 12 to 18 metres with impressive regularity, while green turtles rest on coral heads below. The reef crest is rich in table corals, sea fans, and schooling fusiliers, and the current — when running — pushes divers effortlessly along the wall while attracting pelagics from the deep.
getThere: Boat departure from Gili Trawangan harbour; most dive operators on the island offer daily trips, typically a 5 to 10 minute ride.

name: Halik Reef
description: Halik Reef wraps around the northeast corner of Gili Air and is celebrated for its turtle density — it is not unusual to encounter five or six green turtles in a single dive, resting on barrel sponges or grazing on seagrass patches at the reef base. The shallow top at 5 metres gives way to a sloping wall lined with healthy hard corals, feather stars, and cleaning stations busy with cleaner wrasse. Night dives here reveal lionfish, octopus, and sleeping parrotfish encased in their mucus cocoons.
getThere: Short boat ride from Gili Air harbour, accessible from dive operators based on Gili Air or Gili Trawangan.

name: Gili Trawangan Wall
description: The west-facing wall of Gili Trawangan is a classic Indonesian wall dive, dropping from a coral-crowned lip at 5 metres to a sandy bottom beyond 40 metres. Sea fans the size of dinner tables anchor to the rock face alongside enormous barrel sponges, black coral trees, and gorgonians heavy with crinoids. When the Lombok Strait current runs south, the wall turns into an effortless drift with giant trevally and dogtooth tuna hunting above the blue while nudibranchs and ghost pipefish hide in the coral structure.
getThere: Accessed directly from Gili Trawangan's west beach; dive operators on the island run boat trips to the wall entry point, a 3 to 5 minute ride.

name: Belongas Bay
description: Belongas Bay on Lombok's south coast is one of Indonesia's premier pelagic dive destinations, most famous for the Magnet — a submerged pinnacle at 25 to 40 metres where strong upwellings from the Indian Ocean concentrate hammerhead sharks, oceanic whitetip sharks, and thresher sharks in numbers rarely seen elsewhere in the country. The current is powerful and the site is recommended for experienced divers only, but the reward is extraordinary: schools of hammerheads passing in formation through the blue, often accompanied by silvertip sharks and schools of barracuda.
getThere: Belongas Bay is on Lombok's south coast near Selong Belanak. Most divers arrange liveaboard or day-trip transport from Kuta Lombok, approximately 45 minutes by car then boat.

name: Shark Point
description: Shark Point lies off the southwestern tip of Perhentian Kecil and is the islands' most famous dive, reliably delivering blacktip reef sharks cruising the sandy channel between the reef and open water. The site is a gently sloping reef from 5 to 22 metres, blanketed in branching and massive corals, with a resident population of green and hawksbill turtles that show almost no wariness toward divers. The shallow depth and generally calm conditions make this an excellent all-rounder, though morning dives tend to see the best shark activity before recreational boat traffic increases.

3mm wetsuit — site may be closed due to monsoon
3mm wetsuit — site often closed due to monsoon

getThere: Short speedboat ride from Perhentian Kecil or Perhentian Besar; dive operators on both islands include this site in daily two or three dive packages.

name: Tiga Ruang
description: Tiga Ruang — meaning Three Rooms in Malay — is a dramatic site off the northwest of Perhentian Kecil where three large swim-throughs have been carved into a rocky underwater promontory. The passages are wide enough for comfortable single-file navigation and are draped in soft corals, feather stars, and encrusting sponges. Outside the swim-throughs, the reef is rich in macro subjects: frogfish perch motionless on sponges, ghost pipefish hover in pairs near sea fans, and nudibranchs of exceptional variety dot the rubble zones. The site reaches 25 metres at its deepest and suits both beginners exploring the shallows and more experienced divers pushing into the deeper passages.

3mm wetsuit — site may be closed due to monsoon
3mm wetsuit — site often closed due to monsoon

getThere: Boat from Perhentian Kecil, roughly 10 minutes by speedboat. Most dive operators on both Perhentian islands include Tiga Ruang in macro-focused dive packages.

name: Tokong Laut
description: Tokong Laut — Sea Shrine — is a submerged pinnacle rising from 30 metres to within 8 metres of the surface, positioned on the exposed north side of the Perhentians where open-water currents sweep in from the South China Sea. The pinnacle is encrusted in hard and soft corals, with large sea fans and barrel sponges sheltering schools of snapper, batfish, and fusiliers. Stronger current days bring in eagle rays and the occasional whale shark sighting between May and September. This is one of the more advanced sites in the islands, best dived in settled conditions when visibility can reach 25 metres and beyond.
getThere: Approximately 20 to 25 minutes by speedboat from either Perhentian island. Conditions on the north side can change quickly; operators monitor weather and may redirect to sheltered sites.

name: Batu Nisan
description: Batu Nisan — Tombstone Rock — takes its name from a distinctive upright rock formation that breaks the surface off the southeastern coast of Perhentian Besar. Below the waterline, a sloping reef descends from 3 metres to a sandy floor at 18 metres, dotted with coral bommies that serve as cleaning stations and shelter an exceptional variety of macro life. This is the Perhentians' best dedicated macro and night dive site: blue-ringed octopus have been recorded here, alongside ornate ghost pipefish, harlequin shrimp, and mantis shrimp emerging from sandy burrows after dark. During the day the site is also productive for reef photography given its shallow depth and typically calm conditions.

conditionsByMonth.suitRecommendation: 3mm wetsuit — site may be closed due to monsoon
3mm wetsuit — site may be closed due to monsoon
3mm wetsuit — site often closed due to monsoon

getThere: Short boat ride from Perhentian Besar; many operators on both islands offer dedicated night dive trips to this site, departing at dusk.

name: Manta Bommie
description: A large coral bommie rising from a sandy seabed that acts as a cleaning station for reef manta rays. Mantas glide in regularly to be serviced by wrasse, often circling the structure for extended periods. The bommie itself is draped in hard and soft corals and surrounded by schools of fusiliers, batfish, and the occasional reef shark. Dives here are unhurried — divers hold position and let the mantas come to them.
getThere: Coral Bay is a 1150 km drive north of Perth on the North West Coastal Highway, or fly to Learmonth Airport near Exmouth and drive 80 km south. Most dive operators run boat trips to Manta Bommie from Coral Bay Beach.

name: Five Fingers Reef
description: Five elongated coral fingers stretch from a sandy flat, each rising 4 to 6 metres from the seabed. The channels between them funnel tidal flow and concentrate fish life — schools of snapper pack the gaps and turtles rest on the sand at the base. Table corals dominate the tops while sea fans fill the walls. A straightforward dive at moderate depth that rewards slow exploration.
getThere: Accessible by boat from Coral Bay Beach. Local operators run half-day and full-day reef trips that include Five Fingers Reef as a primary site. The reef lies inside the lagoon and conditions are generally calm.

name: Skeleton Bay
description: A sheltered bay with a mix of coral gardens, rubble patches, and seagrass meadows that draws an unusual collection of macro life. Nudibranch hunters will find species on nearly every dive, and the seagrass beds attract seahorses and pipefish. Rays bury themselves in the sandy margins. A relaxed night dive reveals octopus, cuttlefish, and sleeping reef fish that are easy to approach.
getThere: A short boat ride from Coral Bay Beach, or accessible as a shore dive from the southern end of the beach at low tide. Operators offer dedicated night dive trips here during the summer months.

name: The Labyrinth
description: A maze-like network of coral outcrops and swim-throughs near the outer edge of the Ningaloo lagoon. Coral columns and archways create a three-dimensional dive that rewards confident navigation. Whitetip reef sharks rest in the crevices during the day and reef fish fill every available space. The outer side of the structure picks up more current and occasionally delivers eagle rays and larger pelagics.
getThere: Boat access only from Coral Bay Beach. Operators running outer reef trips include this as a second dive. The site requires basic navigation skills due to the complex coral structure.

name: Navy Pier
description: The Navy Pier at Harold E. Holt Naval Communication Station is consistently ranked among the best shore dives on Earth. The steel piling structure is so heavily encrusted with marine growth it barely resembles a man-made object. Wobbegong sharks pile on top of each other in the shaded corners. Giant Queensland groper cruise the deeper pilings. Lionfish, nudibranchs, moray eels, batfish, and schooling trevally share the same compressed space. Entry requires a permit through a licensed Exmouth dive operator.
getThere: The Navy Pier requires a dive permit obtained through a licensed Exmouth dive operator — independent access is not possible. Operators collect permits and run daily guided shore dives. Exmouth town is 40 km south of the pier. Learmonth Airport serves the region with flights from Perth.

name: Lighthouse Bay
description: A sheltered bay on the western side of the North West Cape with easy shore access and coral bommies scattered across a sandy floor. The site is known for its consistently calm conditions and reliable turtle sightings — green and hawksbill turtles feed on the seagrass and rest on the bommies. Reef fish are prolific and the site is popular for both snorkelling and introductory diving. The protected waters also make it an excellent training site.
getThere: Shore dive from the car park at Lighthouse Bay, 10 km west of Exmouth town via Murat Road. Entry is easy over a sandy beach. No permit required. Operators also run guided dives here as a morning session.

name: Tantabiddi Wall
description: The outer edge of Ningaloo Reef drops steeply here, forming a dramatic wall that begins at 6 metres and falls beyond sport diving limits. Sea fans and black coral line the deeper sections, while the shallower reef top is all hard corals and active fish life. Strong incoming tides push nutrient-rich water up the wall, attracting large schools of fish and triggering feeding frenzies by trevally and mackerel. Whale sharks aggregate nearby during the March to July season.
getThere: Boat access from Tantabiddi Boat Ramp, approximately 30 km northwest of Exmouth via Yardie Creek Road. Local dive operators depart from here. A current hook or reef hook is advisable when current is running on the outer wall.

name: Muiron Islands
description: The North and South Muiron Islands lie 15 km northeast of Exmouth in the Exmouth Gulf and are protected within the Cape Range National Park marine zone. The reefs around both islands are largely pristine, with high coral cover and exceptional visibility. Humpback whales move through the gulf from July to October. Dugongs feed in the seagrass meadows between the islands. The exposed eastern sides deliver drift dives along colourful walls while sheltered western bays offer calmer conditions.
getThere: A 45-minute boat ride from Exmouth Marina or Bundegi Boat Ramp on the Exmouth Gulf side. The trip is weather dependent — open water crossings can be rough in strong southerly winds. Most Exmouth dive operators run day trips to the Muiron Islands by arrangement.

name: HMNZS Canterbury
description: Sunk in 2007 as an artificial reef, the 111-meter Canterbury sits upright at 26 meters in Ngahuia Bay. Penetration-friendly with multiple open decks, the wreck is encrusted with jewel anemones and carpeted in yellow zoanthids. Blue mao mao school through the superstructure and eagle rays circle the stern. One of New Zealand's premier wreck dives.
getThere: Depart from Paihia or Russell wharves; most dive operators run day trips of 30 to 45 minutes to the wreck site.

name: Poor Knights Islands — Rikoriko Cave
description: Rikoriko is one of the largest sea caves in the world, carved into the volcanic tuff of the Poor Knights Islands Marine Reserve. A cathedral-sized chamber fills with filtered blue light at mid-morning. The walls are dense with golden zoanthids, purple urchins, and the endemic demoiselle. Outside the cave, schooling trevally and kingfish patrol the open water above kelp forests draped in orange and crimson nudibranchs.
getThere: Poor Knights lie 24 km northeast of Tutukaka Harbour; day trips depart Tutukaka Marina, roughly 90 minutes south of Paihia.

name: Te Rawhiti Wall
description: A dramatic drop-off on the outer eastern side of the Bay of Islands, Te Rawhiti Wall plunges from 5 meters to beyond 30 meters. The wall face is coated in yellow and orange sponge, jewel anemones, and enormous colonies of encrusting bryozoans. Common dolphins often appear on the surface transit, and orca have been sighted in winter months. Nudibranchs are prolific year-round, making this a macro photographer's wall.
getThere: Accessible by boat from Paihia or Russell; 20 to 30 minute crossing to the eastern outer islands. Most operators run combined wreck and wall itineraries.

name: Hole in the Rock — Motukokako
description: Motukokako (Piercy Island) at the entrance to the Bay of Islands is pierced by a natural rock arch that boats navigate at high tide. Below the surface, the island's base is a terrain of boulder fields, swim-throughs, and short wall sections alive with blue-throated wrasse, marblefish, and banded dottyback. Bottlenose dolphins regularly rest in the sheltered north-facing bay and occasionally interact with divers.
getThere: Boat departure from Paihia or Russell; 45 to 60 minutes to Cape Brett. Cape Brett Walkway permit required for any land visit; divers stay aboard.

name: Teavanui Pass
description: The main passage through Bora Bora's barrier reef, Teavanui funnels strong tidal currents that attract the island's most impressive pelagic encounters. Lemon sharks patrol the sandy channel floor and are joined by blacktip reef sharks, schools of jack, and occasional hammerhead passing through on incoming tide. Eagle rays cruise the current margins. An exhilarating drift for confident divers that builds in intensity with the tide.
getThere: All dive operators on Bora Bora access Teavanui Pass by boat; 10 to 20 minutes from Vaitape wharf. Most operators time entry to incoming tide for the strongest current.

name: Anau Coral Garden
description: A shallow coral garden on the lagoon's northeastern side where hard coral bommies rise from white sand at 5 to 15 meters. Lemon sharks rest in the sand channels between bommies, apparently unbothered by divers, and blacktip reef sharks cruise the perimeter. The site is calm enough for snorkelers but rich enough for experienced divers to spend a full dive exploring coral heads packed with butterflyfish, moorish idols, and resting nurse sharks.
getThere: 15 to 25 minutes by boat from Vaitape; accessible on any day trip from the main island. Also reachable from the eastern motu resorts.

name: Muri Muri
description: A wall site on the lagoon's outer southern edge where the barrier reef drops vertically from 8 meters to 40 meters and beyond. The wall face is encrusted with sea fans, barrel sponges, and field anemones hosting clownfish. Eagle rays and whitetip reef sharks patrol the wall base, and at depth the occasional manta ray passes through between May and October. One of Bora Bora's best sites for wall structure and large animal encounters together.
getThere: Boat required; 25 to 35 minutes from Vaitape. Best dived with a local operator who can time entry to mild current conditions on the outgoing tide.

name: Tupitipiti Point
description: The southwestern tip of Bora Bora's barrier reef where ocean meets lagoon at a dramatic rocky point. Currents here concentrate fish life year-round: dense schools of snapper and surgeonfish, hawksbill turtles feeding on sponge, and grey reef sharks that appear without warning from the blue. In summer months hammerheads have been recorded cruising the deep edge. The terrain — tumbled basalt blocks, coral outcrops, and sand patches — gives divers good structure to shelter behind when currents run hard.
getThere: 30 to 40 minutes by boat from Vaitape. Best approached on outgoing tide to keep current manageable; local operators monitor conditions daily.

name: Tetamanu Wall
description: Just inside the South Pass on the lagoon side, Tetamanu Wall is a sloping coral reef that descends from 6 m at the reef flat to over 30 m into the lagoon. This site rewards slow divers — the wall is carpeted in hard Acropora and Porites corals with dense aggregations of butterflyfish, Moorish idols, and parrotfish grazing the surface. Napoleon wrasse patrol lazily, and large moray eels occupy crevices throughout. The mild current in the lagoon makes this an ideal site for less experienced divers and for those wanting to extend bottom time after a South Pass drift.
getThere: Accessible by boat from Tetamanu village, a 5-minute ride to the inner pass wall. The village has a small lodge and resident dive guide. Day-trip liveaboards from Rotoava reach Tetamanu in roughly 3 hours.

name: Garuae Inner Lagoon
description: The inner lagoon side of Garuae Pass is a gentle drift through a sandy channel flanked by coral bommies and patch reefs rising from 20 m. This is where the big-pass current dissipates into a pleasant 1-knot glide over garden eels swaying in unison from the sand, with blue-spotted stingrays resting between coral heads. Schools of golden trevally and juvenile sharks frequent the shallower bommies. The site is ideal for a second dive after the full Garuae drift and works at all skill levels thanks to the manageable flow inside the lagoon.
getThere: Accessed by boat from Rotoava village, a 5-10 minute ride north along the atoll's western shore to the lagoon entrance of Garuae. All dive operators based in Rotoava offer this site as a standard two-tank morning excursion.

name: Tiahura Shark and Ray Feeding
description: Tiahura is Moorea's most famous dive site and the epicenter of the island's legendary shark and ray encounters. On the sandy floor at 15-18 m, blacktip and lemon sharks circle in loose aggregations alongside marbled stingrays and sometimes a solitary tiger shark. The site has been a structured feeding station for decades, creating habituated sharks that approach closely and provide unparalleled photography opportunities. Coral bommies ring the sand patch with healthy cover of Porites and Acropora, and dense schools of snapper shelter in the gaps.
getThere: Take the ferry from Papeete (Vaiare ferry dock, 30 minutes) or fly to Moorea Airport (MOZ). Dive operators based at Club Bali Hai and along the northwest coast run daily Tiahura shark dives, typically departing at 8:30 and 10:30. Boat ride from northwest shore operators is under 10 minutes.

name: Taotoi Pass
description: Taotoi is a narrow pass cutting through Moorea's northwest reef, funneling tidal flow across a coral-encrusted channel floor between 15 and 25 m. Incoming tides push divers gently into the lagoon past dense aggregations of blue-lined snapper, unicornfish, and paddletail snapper sheltering in the current shadow of large coral heads. Whitetip reef sharks rest on the sandy bottom between surges, and grey reef sharks occasionally patrol the pass mouth on the ocean side. The channel walls are draped in orange and purple sea fans at depth, making it an outstanding wide-angle photography site.
getThere: Dive operators based on Moorea's northwest coast reach Taotoi Pass in 10-15 minutes by boat. The pass is best dived on an incoming tide — operators time departures to match tidal tables. Confirm tidal timing when booking.

name: Opunohu Canyons
description: On the edge of Opunohu Bay, the reef breaks into a series of coral canyons dropping from 15 m to 35 m before meeting the outer slope. The canyon walls are among the healthiest coral formations in Moorea — thick plates of Montipora and branching Acropora colonies with minimal bleaching even in warm years. Lemon sharks rest in the sandy canyon floors and Napoleon wrasse shadow divers throughout the dive. Spinner dolphins regularly transit the bay and occasionally approach divers at the canyon mouth. The site also hosts dense populations of lionfish, nudibranchs, and cleaner shrimp stations in the crevices.
getThere: Boat from operators on the north coast of Moorea, 15-20 minutes to the Opunohu Bay entrance. Operators based at Maharepa or near the ferry dock in Vaiare serve this site. The bay is sheltered and accessible year-round.

name: Tiki Point
description: Tiki Point is a pronounced reef promontory on Moorea's south coast where the outer barrier reef turns sharply and generates consistent mild upwelling. The current brings cooler, nutrient-rich water to a slope covered in enormous sea fans and black coral trees below 25 m, while the shallower terrain above 20 m is a mosaic of hard coral tables and coral heads alive with hawksbill turtles, Moorish idols, and dense wrasse populations. Eagle rays circle the point on most dives, and a resident school of barracuda holds position at 22 m year-round. This is Moorea's best site for large-format underwater photography.
getThere: South coast access requires a 20-25 minute boat ride from Maharepa or the ferry terminal. Fewer operators run south coast trips routinely — book in advance and confirm Tiki Point is on the itinerary. The site is best on a calm day as the south swell can reduce visibility.

name: Coral Gardens
description: Coral Gardens is the signature reef of the Rosario Islands Marine National Park, a sprawling shallow-to-mid-depth system where dense elkhorn and star coral formations shelter an extraordinary density of Caribbean reef fish. French angelfish and queen angelfish patrol the coral heads while schools of blue tang sweep the plateaus. Nurse sharks rest in sandy channels beneath overhanging coral, and spotted eagle rays cruise the outer slope on incoming tide. The park's protected status has allowed coral cover to recover measurably compared to the wider Colombian Caribbean.
getThere: Day boats depart from Cartagena's Muelle de los Pegasos or Embarcadero Turístico; journey takes 45 to 90 minutes depending on sea state. Operators on Isla Grande and Isla del Rosario run guided dives directly.

name: El Tesoro Wreck
description: El Tesoro is a deliberately sunk cargo vessel resting upright at 25 metres, one of the most colonised artificial reefs in the Colombian Caribbean. In the years since scuttling the hull has been claimed by encrusting sponges, black corals, and sea fans, while moray eels occupy every hatch and porthole. Barracuda school above the bridge and a resident green turtle regularly circles the stern. The wreck is diveable at all skill levels — the shallow superstructure tops out at 12 metres, making it an ideal multi-level dive with excellent opportunities for overhead penetration of the cargo holds.
getThere: Day boats from Cartagena reach El Tesoro in under 60 minutes. Most local operators include the wreck as a second dive on morning two-tank trips combined with Coral Gardens.

name: La Cherna Wall
description: La Cherna Wall drops from a coral-encrusted lip at 8 metres to a rubble slope at 35 metres, one of the more dramatic vertical features in the Rosario archipelago. Black coral trees and orange elephant ear sponges anchor the upper wall, while deeper sections host sea fans and large loggerhead sponges. Nassau grouper cruise the mid-wall in the cooler months, and the site is named for the Warsaw grouper — cherna in Spanish — which was historically abundant here and still makes occasional appearances. Caribbean reef sharks are reliably encountered on the blue water edge during outgoing tides.
getThere: Reached via day boat from Cartagena in approximately 75 minutes; often paired with Coral Gardens as part of a two-tank trip. Best dived on an incoming tide when visibility peaks.

name: Playa Blanca Reef
description: Playa Blanca Reef sits in the shallows off Barú Peninsula's famous white sand beach, a long fringing reef platform that makes it one of the easiest entry points into Colombian Caribbean diving. Coral heads of brain, mustard hill, and fire coral support dense populations of sergeant majors, stoplight parrotfish, and banded butterflyfish. Southern stingrays bury in sandy patches between coral heads and are regularly encountered at close range. The site is excellent for snorkellers and new divers — depths rarely exceed 12 metres on the main terrace — while experienced divers explore the reef edge where small reef sharks appear in the late afternoon.
getThere: Playa Blanca is accessible by boat from Cartagena (45 minutes) or by road and boat from the Barú causeway. Shore diving is possible at high tide; boat entry is simpler and more common.

name: La Plata North Wall
description: La Plata North Wall is the primary manta ray cleaning station of Isla de la Plata, where oceanic mantas queue at shallow rocky ridges to be cleaned by angelfish and wrasse. The wall drops from 8 metres to beyond 40 metres with encrusting sponges and black coral, but the real attraction hovers above: giant oceanic mantas with wingspans exceeding 4 metres glide in from open water and circle the cleaning stations with remarkable predictability from June through November. Green sea turtles and Galapagos sea lions also appear in the cooler upwelling months, and whale sharks have been recorded on several occasions during the peak cold-water season.
getThere: Boats depart from Puerto Cayo or Salango, approximately 20 to 30 minutes from Isla de la Plata. The island is within Machalilla National Park; a park fee applies. Operators are based in Puerto López, 2 hours south of Manta by road.

name: La Plata South Pinnacle
description: The South Pinnacle rises from 35 metres to within 12 metres of the surface on the exposed southern tip of Isla de la Plata, channelling strong Humboldt upwellings that attract the most pelagic-dense aggregations around the island. Scalloped hammerheads appear in loose schools during June through September when cold water temperatures peak, while spotted eagle rays sweep the base of the pinnacle in groups. The hard substrate is colonised by black coral and sea fans adapted to the surge, and schools of Moorish idols and creole wrasse swirl around the peak. This is the island's most demanding site — current and surge are significant — but offers the best chance of multi-species pelagic encounters on a single dive.
getThere: Accessed by the same day boats from Puerto López as La Plata North Wall; operators typically run a two-site trip combining North Wall and South Pinnacle. Advanced certification recommended due to currents.

name: Bajo Copé
description: Bajo Copé is a submerged seamount rising to 18 metres, located in open water west of the Ecuadorian coast roughly midway between Manta and La Plata Island. The mount concentrates nutrients in the upwelling zone and acts as a magnet for large pelagics: silky sharks patrol the upper reaches, schools of yellowfin tuna sweep through on feeding runs, and oceanic mantas visit to feed in the plankton-rich water column. Deeper sections of the seamount host large grouper and amberjack. The site is remote and exposed, best suited to experienced divers comfortable with blue-water conditions and significant surge, but the pelagic density on a good day rivals anything in the Eastern Pacific.
getThere: Day trip from Manta port, approximately 90 minutes offshore by speedboat. Dive operators in Manta run dedicated pelagic trips to Bajo Copé; the site is not accessible from Puerto López. Advanced open-water certification required.

name: Los Ahorcados
description: Los Ahorcados — 'the hanged men' — refers to a pair of dramatic rock pinnacles rising from 30 metres to break the surface at the southern extent of Machalilla National Park waters. The pinnacles are draped in black coral, orange cup corals, and encrusting sponges, with dense aggregations of creole fish and surgeonfish moving through the surge zone. Humpback whales pass between the pinnacles on their southward migration from July to September, and their presence underwater is one of the most extraordinary experiences on the Ecuadorian coast. Dive boats time entries carefully around the whales, and sightings of mothers with calves are common in August. Reef sharks patrol the base during ebb tides.
getThere: Day boats from Puerto López reach Los Ahorcados in approximately 40 minutes; the site sits within Machalilla National Park and a park fee is required. Whale season trips (July to September) book up quickly and should be reserved several weeks in advance.

name: Land's End Sea Lion Colony
description: The California sea lion colony at Land's End is one of the most interactive wildlife dives in Mexico. Dozens of curious juveniles spiral around divers, bite at fins, and blow bubble rings inches from your mask. The rocky pinnacles around El Arco form channels with mild surge and a kelp fringe at depth. Visibility is best on incoming tide. Early morning entries beat the glass-bottom boats and catch the colony most active.
getThere: Boat dive from Cabo San Lucas marina, 10 minute ride to Land's End.

name: Sand Falls
description: One of the most unusual dive sites in the Sea of Cortez: an underwater river of white sand cascades off the edge of a submerged plateau and tumbles into deep water, disappearing into the blue. The sand pours continuously over a lip at around 27 m, driven by surge pushing sand from a shallow sandy shelf. The spectacle is best after a mild swell. Divers hover at the lip and watch the river vanish — a genuinely alien environment.
getThere: Boat dive from Cabo marina, 10-15 minutes to the base of El Arco.

name: Pelican Rock
description: Pelican Rock is the beginner-friendly reef of Cabo San Lucas, sheltered inside the bay beneath towering rock spires. Colourful tropical species fill every crevice — king angelfish, pufferfish, moray eels, and the ubiquitous Cortez rainbow wrasse. Depths stay shallow and the surge is gentle, making it ideal for new divers or those who want to slow down and look at small things. Night diving here reveals octopus, hermit crabs, and sleeping parrotfish.
getThere: Boat dive from Cabo marina, 5 minutes into the bay.

name: Gordo Banks
description: Gordo Banks is an offshore seamount system rising from 200 m to within 27 m of the surface, positioned at the convergence of Pacific and Sea of Cortez currents. This nutrient upwelling makes it the best site in Cabo for large pelagics: scalloped hammerhead sharks aggregate in significant numbers from June through November, whale sharks appear June through September, and oceanic manta rays patrol the blue water column. The dive is current-dependent and conditions change quickly — advanced certification and a good briefing required.
getThere: Liveaboard or long day-boat trip from Cabo marina, approximately 45 minutes by panga.

name: Islas Marietas
description: The Islas Marietas are a protected UNESCO-recognised national park 35 km offshore, formed by volcanic collapse. The submerged lava tunnels and arches shelter massive schools of fish and a dense reef community. The surface-famous Hidden Beach is above water — the diving equivalent is the swim-throughs and caverns beneath the waterline, home to white-tipped reef sharks resting on sandy floors. Giant manta rays are regular visitors at the cleaning stations on the exposed northern faces.
getThere: Day boat from Puerto Vallarta marina or Punta de Mita, approximately 45 minutes to 1 hour.

name: El Morro
description: El Morro is an exposed rocky headland near the tip of Punta de Mita that funnels current and concentrates marine life in the northern reaches of Banderas Bay. The site is best known for giant manta rays — sometimes 20 or more in a single session — that come to cleaning stations on the rock faces. Scalloped hammerheads visit in the deeper blue water off the point. The reef structure itself is richly encrusted and reliably productive for photography.
getThere: Boat from Punta de Mita or Puerto Vallarta marina, 20-40 minutes depending on departure point.

name: Los Arcos
description: Los Arcos Marine Sanctuary sits just south of Puerto Vallarta where a cluster of granitic rock formations jut from the sea. The arches and swim-throughs give the site its name, and the protected status has allowed the reef to recover beautifully. Schools of surgeonfish, big eye jacks, and Pacific creolefish fill the water column. Sea turtles are reliable visitors, green and hawksbill both, and moray eels pack the crevices. A shallower site perfect for all levels.
getThere: Short boat ride from Puerto Vallarta marina or Mismaloya beach, 10-20 minutes.

name: La Corbeteña
description: La Corbeteña is a remote offshore seamount rising from 200 m to 25 m below the surface, sitting 27 km southwest of Puerto Vallarta in open Pacific. The seamount is too deep for recreational reef diving on its upper shelf but the walls and blue water draw extraordinary pelagics: bull sharks, silky sharks, silvertip sharks, massive schools of bigeye trevally, and seasonal whale sharks. This is a serious advanced site requiring a long boat ride and current experience — when conditions align, it competes with the best seamount dives in the Pacific.
getThere: Long day-boat or liveaboard from Puerto Vallarta marina, 1.5 to 2 hours each way. Advanced divers only.

name: Ogden Point Breakwater
description: Victoria's most accessible shore dive runs 800 m along a granite breakwater wall that drops to 18 m and shelters an explosion of invertebrate life. Giant Pacific octopus patrol the rubble at the base, wolf eels occupy crevices, and decorator crabs festoon themselves with hydroids. Plumose anemone colonies — white and orange — carpet the granite blocks in densities that rival any temperate reef in the world. Current sweeps along the outer face, delivering plankton and creating a drift effect on the incoming tide.
getThere: Ogden Point is a 10-minute drive from downtown Victoria on Dallas Road. Street parking is free along the seawall. Dive Victoria operates a compressor station and equipment rental at the site.

name: Race Rocks Ecological Reserve
description: Race Rocks is a protected ecological reserve 20 km southwest of Victoria where tidal currents through the Strait of Juan de Fuca create one of the most productive cold-water ecosystems on the BC coast. Steller sea lions haul out on the rocks by the hundreds and dive with boats in the water. Harbour seals, California sea lions, and river otters share the reserve with enormous lingcod, cabezon, and the occasional Pacific white-sided dolphin. The rocky pinnacles and boulders drop to 25 m and are encrusted with strawberry anemones and purple sea urchins.
getThere: Race Rocks is accessible only by boat from Victoria Harbour or Pedder Bay Marina in Metchosin. The crossing takes 20 to 45 minutes depending on departure point. A permit is not required for recreational diving but boats must anchor outside the hauling zones. Dive charters depart from Victoria daily in summer.

name: Ten Mile Point
description: Ten Mile Point juts into Haro Strait near Cadboro Bay, creating a rocky headland with exceptional wall diving down to 30 m. The walls are draped in cloud sponge, boot sponge, and dense colonies of orange cup coral — species normally found much deeper on the open coast. Giant Pacific octopus are resident year-round and wolf eels occupy dens in the boulder fields at depth. Currents running along the point bring cold upwelled water and push visibility above 15 m in winter. Advanced divers use the outgoing tide for a controlled drift along the kelp wall.
getThere: Ten Mile Point is off Baynes Road in Saanich, a 15-minute drive from downtown Victoria. Park at the Cattle Point trailhead or along Tudor Avenue and follow the shoreline trail 5 minutes to the point. Entry is from the rocky beach at slack tide.

name: HMCS Mackenzie Wreck
description: The HMCS Mackenzie, a 111 m Canadian destroyer escort, was deliberately sunk in 1995 in Saanich Inlet near Saltspring Island as an artificial reef. Sitting upright at 30 m on a sandy bottom in Satellite Channel, it is one of the best wreck dives on the BC coast. The hull is encrusted with giant plumose anemones, cloud sponge, and colonial tunicates. Giant Pacific octopus inhabit the superstructure, wolf eels guard the torpedo tubes, and lingcod hold court in the engine room openings. A second wreck, the HMCS Herons, lies nearby and can be combined on a single dive.
getThere: The HMCS Mackenzie is accessed by boat from Maple Bay Marina or Cowichan Bay on Vancouver Island, or from Salt Spring Island. The crossing takes 20 to 30 minutes. A mooring buoy marks the bow. Live-aboard charters and day trip operators run from Victoria and Nanaimo.

name: Turn Island State Park
description: Turn Island Marine State Park sits just east of Friday Harbor on San Juan Island, surrounded by a protected marine waters area. Rocky reefs at 12 to 22 m are carpeted with giant Pacific octopus dens, white and orange plumose anemones, and thick beds of purple sea urchins. Bull kelp forests grow to 15 m at the south end of the island and shelter lingcod, cabezon, and schools of black rockfish. The tidal channel between Turn Island and San Juan Island produces gentle drift conditions on the slack, making it ideal for intermediate divers who want their first taste of Pacific Northwest cold water.
getThere: Turn Island is a 5-minute kayak or boat ride from Friday Harbor on San Juan Island. Access the water from the Jackson Beach boat launch or Friday Harbor Marina. Diving is done from an anchored boat or kayak. Washington State Ferries serve Friday Harbor from Anacortes on the mainland with multiple daily sailings.

name: Lime Kiln Point State Park
description: Lime Kiln Point on the west side of San Juan Island overlooks Haro Strait, one of the primary corridors used by the Southern Resident killer whale population. From the surface, orca are visible multiple times per week in summer. Below, the basalt walls plunge from the cobble beach to 30 m through kelp forest and into open rock draped with strawberry anemones and boot sponge. Giant Pacific octopus dens dot the wall. The site is exposed to Haro Strait swells and the current can reach 3 knots, so timing entry to the slack is essential.
getThere: Lime Kiln Point State Park is on Westside Road, a 15-minute drive from Friday Harbor. There is a day-use parking fee. Entry is from the cobble beach below the lighthouse. Dive only on the slack — the Whale Watch Park tide tables published by NOAA give precise turn times for Haro Strait.

name: Deadman's Bay
description: Deadman's Bay on the northwest end of San Juan Island is a sheltered kelp-walled cove where the current is reduced compared to the exposed west shore. Rocky reefs step down to 20 m through bull kelp forests thick with school of black rockfish and copper rockfish. Giant Pacific octopus are abundant — this site has one of the highest encounter rates in the San Juan Islands. Wolf eels share the boulder fields at depth. The protected aspect makes it one of the more forgiving entry points on the island, though a drysuit is still essential.
getThere: Deadman's Bay is accessible from English Camp National Historical Park on the north end of San Juan Island via West Valley Road, approximately 20 minutes from Friday Harbor. Park at the English Camp area and walk to the cove. Shore entry from the gravel beach.

name: Eagle Point, Orcas Island
description: Eagle Point on the southeastern tip of Orcas Island is a rocky headland where the seafloor plunges quickly to 28 m and the walls are covered in thick carpets of giant plumose anemones, encrusting sponge, and colonial tunicates. Giant Pacific octopus are regularly found in the boulder zone at 10 to 18 m. Schools of pile perch and black rockfish hold in the kelp just off the point. This is a boat-access site with moderate current on the tidal exchange, and one of the more remote and pristine dive sites in the archipelago — orca transiting Rosario Strait are visible from the surface.
getThere: Eagle Point is boat-access only, departing from Deer Harbor Marina or West Sound on Orcas Island. The crossing takes 15 minutes. Orcas Island is reached by Washington State Ferries from Anacortes. Dive charters operate from Deer Harbor and Eastsound.

name: Larvotto Marine Reserve
description: Established in 1976 and straddling the border between Monaco and Nice, the Larvotto reserve is the most protected stretch of coastline on the French Riviera. Decades without fishing have allowed dusky grouper to grow to trophy size and red scorpionfish to colonise every rocky ledge from the shallows to 40 metres. Yellow gorgonian fans line the sloping reef walls and sea fans crowd the overhangs where large morays reside year-round. The reserve is accessible by short boat ride from Nice or as a shore dive from Monaco's Larvotto beach.
getThere: Fly into Nice Cote d'Azur Airport (NCE); the Larvotto reserve is about 20 minutes by road east toward Monaco. Several dive centres operate from Nice port and from Monaco's Fontvieille harbour. Boat dives take 15 to 30 minutes to reach the reserve. Shore access is possible from the Larvotto beach in Monaco.

name: Cap Ferrat Wall
description: The submarine extension of the Cap Ferrat peninsula drops as a sheer limestone wall from 10 to 60 metres, bristling with red and yellow gorgonian fans that grow to over a metre in diameter on the deeper sections. Dusky grouper patrol mid-water, large moray eels coil in the wall's fissures, and swarms of anthias create a curtain of orange above the sea fans. The wall's north-facing aspect keeps it shaded and cool, and visibility is reliably excellent from May through October. This is the premier wall dive on the Nice coast.
getThere: Cap Ferrat is 10 kilometres east of Nice; dive operators from Nice port and Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat village both serve the wall. The drive from Nice Cote d'Azur Airport takes about 25 minutes. Boat journey to the dive site is approximately 10 to 15 minutes from Saint-Jean. No shore access.

name: Riou Canyon
description: A submarine canyon cutting into the continental shelf south of Nice, Riou draws advanced divers for its dramatic geology and the pelagic life that aggregates along its rim. The canyon walls begin at around 30 metres and plunge beyond recreational limits; on the plateau leading to the edge, large dentex and amberjack cruise in open water while nudibranchs and sponges carpet every horizontal surface. The deeper sections hold cold, blue water with exceptional visibility. Mild drift conditions along the canyon edge make this an exhilarating dive for experienced open-water divers.
getThere: Riou Canyon is 12 to 15 kilometres offshore from Nice; access is by dive boat only and journey times are approximately 30 to 40 minutes. Only experienced operators with open-water navigation capability run trips here; most are based out of Nice port or Antibes. Advanced open water certification minimum.

name: Lerin Islands Plateau
description: Off the shore of Cannes, the Lerin Islands — Sainte-Marguerite and Saint-Honorat — sit atop a shallow limestone plateau that transitions into spectacular rocky reefs colonised by sponges, gorgonians, and dense populations of sea bream, wrasse, and octopus. The site is sheltered from prevailing south-westerly swells and remains diveable much of the year. Posidonia meadows in the bays between the islands support cuttlefish and long-snouted seahorses, making it one of the most ecologically diverse sites on the Cote d'Azur. Night dives here reveal a population of red scorpionfish hunting across the reef.
getThere: The Lerin Islands are a 15-minute ferry from Cannes port; Cannes is 30 kilometres west of Nice by road or 30 minutes by train. Dive operators in Cannes run boat dives to the islands directly. The site is approximately 25 minutes by dive boat from Antibes. Some dive centres run day trips from Nice, adding about 30 minutes of transit.

name: Starfish Island Reef
description: The sloping reef circling Starfish Island is one of Honda Bay's most-visited sites, and for good reason. Coral tables shelter resting nurse sharks in 6 to 12 metres, while the outer slope descends through bommies of staghorn and brain coral to a rubble and sand bottom at 22 metres. Large cushion starfish (the site's namesake) cover the sandy shallows. Bumphead parrotfish arrive in loose schools at dawn, and sea turtles are spotted year-round on the coral terraces.
getThere: Take a tricycle or van from Puerto Princesa city (35 minutes) to Santa Lourdes Wharf, then a 20 to 30 minute bangka boat ride to the island. Day trips are standard; most operators depart 8am.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Direct flights from Manila (1h10m) and Cebu. Airport is 10 km from the city centre.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesName: Santa Lourdes Wharf to Starfish Island
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: Tricycle or van to Santa Lourdes Wharf (35 min), then bangka boat (20 to 30 min). Wharf departure typically 8am for day trips.

name: Cowrie Island Reef
description: Cowrie Island's reef wraps around a small islet ringed by mangroves and delivers some of the best shallow hard-coral coverage in Honda Bay. Massive Porites boulders rise from a sandy floor at 18 metres, and the upper reef crest is blanketed with healthy table corals and fields of staghorn. Juvenile fish density is exceptionally high, making this a paradise for macro shooters. Reef whitetip sharks patrol the outer rim and banded sea snakes weave through coral crevices.
getThere: Depart from Santa Lourdes Wharf by bangka (25 minutes). Most Honda Bay day trips include Cowrie Island as one of three island stops.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Direct flights from Manila (1h10m) and Cebu. Airport is 10 km from the city centre.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesName: Santa Lourdes Wharf to Cowrie Island
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: Tricycle from Puerto Princesa to Santa Lourdes Wharf (35 min), then bangka boat (25 min). Standard island-hopping tours include this stop.

name: Pandan Island Wall
description: The east face of Pandan Island drops in a dramatic vertical wall from 5 metres to beyond 35 metres, festooned with gorgonian sea fans, black coral trees, and thick carpets of soft coral. Large pelagics including Napoleon wrasse, dogtooth tuna, and occasional barracuda schools cruise the blue water beyond the wall top. This is the most demanding site in Honda Bay, with a moderate surge on the wall face during southwesterly months and occasional thermoclines below 25 metres.
getThere: Charter a private bangka from Santa Lourdes Wharf (40 to 50 minutes). This site is not usually included on standard island-hopping tours; request it specifically from a dive operator in Puerto Princesa.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Direct flights from Manila (1h10m) and Cebu. Airport is 10 km from the city centre.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesName: Santa Lourdes Wharf to Pandan Island
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: Private bangka charter from Santa Lourdes Wharf (40 to 50 min). Book through a Puerto Princesa dive shop; not included on standard day tours.

name: Luli Island Nurse Shark Flats
description: Luli Island (its name means "half submerged" in Filipino) is surrounded by sandy flats and seagrass meadows that shelter the largest congregation of nurse sharks in Honda Bay. Multiple tawny nurse sharks rest motionless under coral outcrops through the day, easily approached to within a few metres. The adjacent seagrass beds host dugong feeding trails, and sea turtles are regularly seen grazing. Depths stay shallow, making this a perfect first-dive-of-the-day site and an ideal location for underwater photography in natural light.
getThere: Bangka from Santa Lourdes Wharf (15 to 20 minutes). Luli Island is a regular stop on Honda Bay island-hopping tours. Arrive early morning for the best nurse shark sightings before day-trip crowds arrive.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Direct flights from Manila (1h10m) and Cebu. Airport is 10 km from the city centre.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesName: Santa Lourdes Wharf to Luli Island
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: Tricycle from Puerto Princesa to Santa Lourdes Wharf (35 min), then bangka boat (15 to 20 min). Included on most Honda Bay island-hopping day tours.

name: Sohoton Jellyfish Lake
description: Hidden inside the limestone karst of Bucas Grande island, Sohoton Cove's marine lake is one of the world's few places where divers and snorkellers can swim freely among thousands of stingless jellyfish (Mastigias papua etpisoni). The lake connects to the sea through underwater tunnels that regulate salinity and temperature, creating a brackish environment where the jellies have lost their sting through evolutionary isolation. Morning light pierces the jungle canopy and illuminates shafts of pulsing jellyfish. Snorkelling is more common than scuba here to minimise bubble disturbance, and the caves above the waterline hold ancient boat coffins.
getThere: From General Luna (Siargao), hire a speedboat or join a tour to Bucas Grande (45 to 60 minutes). Enter the cove by paddle canoe during high tide when the passage is navigable. Permits required; guides are mandatory. Jellyfish presence is seasonal and can diminish after storms.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Flights from Cebu (40 min) and Manila (90 min). Airport is 30 km from General Luna township.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: Speedboat from General Luna to Bucas Grande (45 to 60 min), then paddle canoe into the cove. Tour operators handle permits and mandatory guides.

name: Tayangban Cave Pool
description: Tayangban Cave on Bucas Grande island is a cathedral-sized limestone cavern whose interior hosts a brackish pool connected by tidal passages to the open sea. Divers enter through a low-ceilinged underwater entrance and surface inside a vast vaulted chamber draped with stalactites and draped in filtered green light. The cave walls are home to endemic cave shrimp and translucent fish species found nowhere else. This site combines spelunking and diving into a single experience and requires a guide; the passages are narrow and depth is limited but the atmosphere is extraordinary.
getThere: Combined with a Sohoton Cove day trip. Speedboat from General Luna (45 to 60 minutes), then wade or swim into the cave entrance. Low tide can restrict entry; operators time trips around tides. Mandatory guide and helmet required.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Flights from Cebu (40 min) and Manila (90 min). Airport is 30 km from General Luna.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: Speedboat from General Luna to Bucas Grande (45 to 60 min). Usually combined with Sohoton Cove on the same day trip. Guide and helmet mandatory.

name: Daco Island Reef
description: Daco Island sits southeast of General Luna and is ringed by a mosaic of reef, rubble, and sandy muck that is arguably the best macro diving in Siargao. Pygmy seahorses cling to sea fans at 18 to 22 metres, and the sandy channels between coral heads host blue-ringed octopus, ornate ghost pipefish, and a diversity of nudibranch species that draws underwater macro photographers from across the Philippines. The reef crest holds healthy staghorn and Acropora thickets with clownfish anemone gardens and schools of anthias.
getThere: Bangka from General Luna dock (20 to 25 minutes). Daco Island is one of Siargao's three famous sand-bar islands and sees regular boat traffic; dive operators in General Luna run dedicated macro trips here.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Flights from Cebu (40 min) and Manila (90 min). Airport is 30 km from General Luna.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: Bangka from General Luna dock (20 to 25 min). Dive operators in General Luna run regular macro trips; island-hopping boats also stop here.

name: Naked Island Channel
description: The tidal channel between Naked Island and the surrounding islets funnels current-rich water and concentrates schooling fish in impressive numbers. Jacks, fusiliers, and surgeonfish form dense tornados in the mid-water column while grey reef sharks patrol the channel floor at 18 to 28 metres. During whale shark season (March to May) the channel is a reliable aggregation point; whale shark encounters are frequent with 30 to 45 minute sightings at the surface and shallow dives. The reef along the channel walls is in excellent condition with thick soft-coral growth.
getThere: Bangka from General Luna dock (25 to 30 minutes). Standard island-hopping trips pass through the channel; dedicated drift dives and whale shark excursions are offered by General Luna dive operators March through May.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Flights from Cebu (40 min) and Manila (90 min). Airport is 30 km from General Luna.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesName: General Luna to Naked Island Channel
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: Bangka from General Luna dock (25 to 30 min). Standard island-hopping includes a stop here; dive operators run dedicated drift and whale shark trips March through May.

name: Batu Angus
description: Batu Angus — meaning 'burned rock' — is a lava field created by Gamalama's 1673 eruption that extends beneath the surface as a dramatic geological landscape. Volcanic boulders encrusted with tunicates and hydroids shelter pygmy seahorses, ghost pipefish, and frogfish. The black lava substrate makes colours pop for macro photography and the site is rarely dived.
getThere: Fly to Sultan Babullah Airport (TTE) in Ternate via Makassar or Manado. Local dive operators in Ternate town arrange boat transfers to Batu Angus on the island's north coast, approximately 20 minutes by speedboat.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Sultan Babullah Airport served by Wings Air from Manado (45 min) and Makassar (2 hrs). Daily connections available.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: Local dive operators run 20-minute speedboat transfers to Batu Angus on the north coast. No public boat service to dive sites.

name: Tomagoba
description: A black sand muck site on Ternate's southwest coast that rivals the best of Lembeh for critter diversity. The volcanic sediment is home to mimic octopus, wunderpus, flamboyant cuttlefish, and a remarkable variety of nudibranchs. Night dives here are exceptional, with coconut octopus emerging to hunt across the dark substrate.
getThere: Fly to Sultan Babullah Airport (TTE) in Ternate. Dive operators from Ternate town run 15-minute speedboat transfers to Tomagoba on the southwest coast. The site is best dived in the morning before wind builds.
