getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Sultan Babullah Airport served by Wings Air from Manado (45 min) and Makassar (2 hrs). Daily connections available.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: 15-minute speedboat ride from Ternate town harbour. Operators can arrange early-morning departures to catch calm conditions before afternoon winds.

name: Kastela Wall
description: A spectacular vertical reef wall on Ternate's southwest side that drops from 5 metres to beyond 60 metres, carpeted in sea fans, black coral trees, and dense soft coral gardens. The wall faces the open Molucca Sea and attracts pelagic visitors including schooling jacks, napoleon wrasse, and passing whitetip reef sharks. One of Ternate's signature wide-angle dives.
getThere: Fly to Sultan Babullah Airport (TTE) in Ternate. Kastela Wall is on the island's southwest coast, approximately 25 minutes by speedboat from Ternate town. Dive operators arrange guided boat trips.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Sultan Babullah Airport served by Wings Air from Manado (45 min) and Makassar (2 hrs). Daily connections available.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: 25-minute speedboat transfer from Ternate town harbour. Site is best dived on incoming tide when visibility peaks.

name: Sulamadaha Point
description: A rocky headland on Ternate's northwest coast where the volcanic reef meets strong upwelling currents, creating a feeding frenzy of reef fish and drawing in larger pelagics. Pristine staghorn and table coral gardens in the shallows give way to a colourful wall teeming with anthias and basslets. Bumphead parrotfish regularly visit in formation at dawn.
getThere: Fly to Sultan Babullah Airport (TTE) in Ternate. Sulamadaha Point is on the northwest coast, 20 minutes from Ternate town by speedboat. Best dived at slack water — dive operators advise on tidal timing.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Sultan Babullah Airport served by Wings Air from Manado (45 min) and Makassar (2 hrs). Daily connections available.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: 20-minute speedboat transfer from Ternate town. Current can be strong — operators always brief tidal windows before departure.

name: Cape Nelson Wreck
description: A Japanese WWII cargo vessel sunk during Allied operations around Cape Nelson in 1943, now resting at 28 to 42 metres on a sloping sandy bottom. The wreck is heavily encrusted with black corals, feather stars, and sea fans, and shelters large schools of glassfish, batfish, and juvenile sweetlips. A bow gun remains in situ and the holds are penetrable with a dive light.
getThere: Fly to Tufi via Port Moresby or Popondetta. Tufi Resort is the main base and operates all dive trips — transfers are included with dive packages. The wreck is a 20-minute boat ride from the resort jetty.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Jacksons International Airport. Fly POM to Tufi (TFI) via Susi Air or charter — approximately 1 hour. Alternative: fly POM to Popondetta (PNP) then road transfer (3 hrs) or light aircraft to Tufi.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: Tufi Resort provides all dive boat transfers. 20-minute ride to the Cape Nelson wreck site. No independent dive access — all dives booked through the resort.

name: Tufi Fjord Wall
description: The drowned river valley walls of Tufi's fjords plunge vertically from the surface to depths beyond 50 metres, draped in a near-unbroken blanket of soft corals, sea fans, and wire corals. The sheltered fjord water is remarkably clear and calm year-round, making this the ideal site for both novice and experienced divers. Pygmy seahorses, Spanish dancer nudibranchs, and mandarin fish all reside within the wall's crevices.
getThere: Fly to Tufi via Port Moresby. Tufi Resort operates all dives — the fjord wall sites are 5 to 10 minutes by boat from the resort jetty and are regularly included in the house reef programme.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Jacksons International Airport. Fly POM to Tufi (TFI) via Susi Air or charter — approximately 1 hour.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: 5 to 10-minute boat ride from the resort. Fjord walls are included in morning and afternoon dive schedules daily.

name: Rainbow Passage
description: A narrow channel between two fjord walls where tidal flow accelerates and concentrates fish life into a dense, colourful spectacle. Schooling anthias, fusiliers, and glassfish fill the water column while giant grouper and dogtooth tuna patrol the current lines. The passage walls are encrusted with basket sponges, wire coral, and massive sea fans rivalling anything in the Coral Triangle.
getThere: Fly to Tufi via Port Moresby. Tufi Resort runs all dive operations. Rainbow Passage is 15 minutes by boat from the resort. Dives are timed to tidal flow — operators brief entry windows at the morning dive meeting.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Jacksons International Airport. Fly POM to Tufi (TFI) via Susi Air or charter — approximately 1 hour.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: 15-minute boat ride. Drift dives are timed to tidal flow — the resort schedules Rainbow Passage based on optimal current windows each day.

name: Shark Point
description: A exposed headland at the mouth of the Tufi fjord system where the open Solomon Sea delivers a steady supply of pelagic life. Whitetip and grey reef sharks patrol the point in numbers, while hammerheads are sighted on early morning dives. The top of the point is smothered in pristine hard coral and the drop-off on the south side features enormous barrel sponges.
getThere: Fly to Tufi via Port Moresby. Shark Point is 25 minutes by resort boat from Tufi Resort. The site is weather-dependent and only accessed when the Solomon Sea is calm — operators check conditions daily.

getThereStructured.nearestHubDescription: Jacksons International Airport. Fly POM to Tufi (TFI) via Susi Air or charter — approximately 1 hour.
getThereStructured.transferToSitesDescription: 25-minute boat ride to the exposed headland. Weather and sea state permitting only — Tufi Resort confirms site access at the morning dive briefing.

name: Les Avirons Wall
description: A sheer volcanic wall on Reunion's southwest coast, Les Avirons drops from 6 metres at the reef top to beyond 50 metres, its basalt face colonised by black coral trees, large sea fans, and aggregations of soldierfish sheltering in the overhangs. Bull sharks are a regular presence along the wall base, and Napoleon wrasse cruise the shallower sections with characteristic calm. The wall's volcanic origin means the rock face itself is visually striking — dark, textured lava interrupted by crevices packed with invertebrate life.
getThere: Access by boat from Saint-Leu dive operators, approximately 10 minutes offshore. Shore entry is possible but the boat route is standard.

name: La Grande Anse Pinnacles
description: Volcanic spires rise from a sandy floor at 28 metres, their sides encrusted with cup corals and crinoids, the surrounding water frequently patrolled by hammerhead sharks during austral winter. The pinnacles create natural current breaks that concentrate reef fish — large schools of snapper and fusilier wheel around the formations while grouper hold in the gaps. Between November and March, humpback whales are sometimes audible during the dive, passing through on migration.
getThere: Boat dive from Saint-Pierre or Petite-Ile operators, approximately 15 to 20 minutes by RIB from the nearest launch point.

name: Tombant de la Possession
description: One of Reunion's most celebrated wall dives, this vertical drop-off on the northwest coast begins in shallow coral gardens and plunges into open blue. The wall face is dressed in large gorgonian fans and barrel sponges, and at depth the silhouette of bull sharks moving below is a regular occurrence. Sea turtles are common in the upper 15 metres, feeding on the seagrass patches and resting in the coral ledges. The site rewards slow, methodical divers who take time with the wall's smaller residents — nudibranchs, flatworms, and ornate ghost pipefish.
getThere: Boat departure from La Possession harbour or Saint-Denis area dive centres. The site sits roughly 5 minutes offshore at the base of the coastal cliffs.

name: Cap La Houssaye
description: The reef and wall system at Cap La Houssaye on Reunion's northwest coast is the island's most photogenic shallow dive — a lava shelf at 5 to 12 metres gives way to a moderate wall draped in soft coral and wire coral, where lionfish hover in the shadows and trumpet fish hang vertically in plain sight. The protected bay sees calmer conditions than the exposed south coast sites, making it ideal for night dives when octopus, squid, and sleeping turtles are visible in the torch beam. Reef whitetip sharks rest on the sandy bottom during the day.
getThere: Shore entry is possible from the road pullout at Cap La Houssaye, or by short boat transfer from Saint-Paul dive operators. Shore entry suits divers comfortable navigating lava rock.

name: Baixa do Sul
description: A submerged volcanic bank off Terceira's south coast, Baixa do Sul tops out at 18 metres and falls away into open Atlantic water beyond 50 metres. The plateau draws mobula rays in summer — sometimes in squadrons of 30 or more — and blue sharks appear around the edges of the bank with regularity from June onward. The hard substrate is carpeted in encrusting sponges and lace coral, and common dolphins occasionally dive down to investigate divers at shallower depths. The site demands a live boat due to surface swells and current.
getThere: Boat only. Angra do Heroismo is the main departure point, approximately 20 minutes by fast RIB. Surface conditions can be rough — confirm sea state with the operator before committing.

name: Pico do Ambrosio
description: A volcanic seamount pinnacle off Terceira's northeast coast rising from 60 metres to within 22 metres of the surface, Pico do Ambrosio is the island's signature big animal dive. The summit and flanks are thick with yellow and orange gorgonian sea fans, large black coral trees, and aggregations of bream and wrasse. Blue sharks appear reliably in summer, often circling the pinnacle tip at mid-water depth. Bottlenose dolphins are a consistent presence, and sperm whales have been documented in the deeper water surrounding the seamount during spring.
getThere: Boat only from Praia da Vitoria or Angra do Heroismo. Journey time is approximately 25 to 35 minutes depending on conditions. Advanced open water certification minimum; current experience strongly recommended.

name: Caverna das Focas
description: Named for the Atlantic grey seals that historically used this stretch of the Terceira coast, Caverna das Focas is a volcanic cave and arch system that penetrates the cliffline to a depth of 22 metres. The cavern interior is decorated with encrusting sponges in vivid orange and purple, and the archway frames a fish-soup exterior of bream, wrasse, and comber. Conger eels occupy the deeper cave sections, and the resident population of cleaner wrasse services a steady queue of passing visitors. Light play through the cave mouth makes this a rewarding photography site.
getThere: Shore entry from a marked access point on the northwest coast road, or boat transfer from Angra do Heroismo. Shore entry involves a 5 minute surface swim from a rocky ledge entry.

name: Ilheu das Cabras
description: The twin islets of Ilheu das Cabras off Terceira's southeast coast form a protected marine reserve, and the difference is visible the moment you enter the water — fish density is notably higher here than at unprotected sites. The channel between the two islets funnels current and concentrates planktivores: large schools of salema and bream orbit the rocky walls while moray eels peer from crevices and starfish cover the lower reef. Blue sharks occasionally enter the channel during summer. The site is accessible enough for intermediate divers in settled conditions but surges strongly when swell wraps around from the south.
getThere: Short boat transfer from Angra do Heroismo harbour, approximately 10 to 15 minutes. The islets are visible from the coast and some operators offer a swim-in option on very calm days.

name: Crystal Bay
description: Crystal Bay is Nusa Penida's most celebrated dive site and the world's premier location to encounter the ocean sunfish (mola mola). A sheltered bay opens onto a submerged pinnacle that drops steeply to 40 m, where cleaning stations in the 18–30 m range attract mola mola ascending from the deep Lombok Strait thermocline between July and October. Cold upwellings (sometimes as low as 16°C) roll in from the south, creating a thermocline shock that keeps the site productive but demands a thick wetsuit. Outside mola mola season the site still rewards with coral gardens, sweetlips, and the occasional reef shark. Currents are mild in the bay but can surge on the outer pinnacle.
getThere: Depart from Sanur Beach, Bali by fast boat (approximately 45 minutes) or public ferry to Nusa Penida. Crystal Bay is on the northwest coast of Nusa Penida island, reached by local dive boat from Toyapakeh or Penida harbour.

name: Manta Point
description: Manta Point on the southwest coast of Nusa Penida is one of the most reliable manta ray cleaning stations in Southeast Asia. Reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) congregate year-round at a series of shallow cleaning stations between 5 and 18 m depth, where small cleaner wrasse service them in circuits. The site is exposed to Indian Ocean swell and current, so conditions can shift quickly — surface chop and downwellings are common. When conditions align the water turns a vivid blue and dozens of mantas stack up at the cleaning station simultaneously. Snorkelling is also popular here. Diving is best in the dry season when visibility peaks.
getThere: Fast boat from Sanur Beach, Bali (45 minutes) or from Nusa Penida harbour. Manta Point is on the exposed southwest coast; dive operators in Toyapakeh and Penida town run daily trips when sea conditions allow.

name: Toyapakeh
description: Toyapakeh sits on the northwest tip of Nusa Penida where the Lombok Strait narrows and tidal currents accelerate dramatically, making this one of the most exhilarating drift dives in Bali. The site is a wide sloping reef that falls from the shallows to a sandy bottom at around 30 m, studded with hard coral formations and patrolled by large schools of fusiliers, trevally, and barracuda. Strong currents carry divers along the reef at pace, and the upwellings bring cold, nutrient-rich water that sustains dense fish life. Garden eels carpet the sandy patches between coral heads. Timing the current window is critical — this site demands experience with drift diving.
getThere: Toyapakeh village on the northwest coast of Nusa Penida is one of the main ferry arrival points from Sanur and Padang Bai, Bali. Dive operators are based at the waterfront and boats launch directly from the bay.

name: Gamat Bay
description: Gamat Bay is one of Nusa Penida's more sheltered sites, making it an excellent choice when currents are running hard elsewhere. The bay features gently sloping coral gardens transitioning to a wall on its eastern edge, with pristine hard and soft coral communities that escaped the coral bleaching events more severely felt on other sites. Macro life is exceptional here — pygmy seahorses, ornate ghost pipefish, nudibranchs, and frogfish reward patient divers. The sheltered nature of the bay makes it suitable for all experience levels and a favoured morning dive before operators move to the more demanding sites. Night dives reveal mandarin fish, octopus, and hunting lionfish.
getThere: Gamat Bay is on the north coast of Nusa Penida, a short boat ride from Toyapakeh. Access is by dive boat only; operators from Toyapakeh or Penida town include it in multi-site day trips.

name: Verde Island Drop-Off
description: Verde Island Drop-Off is the flagship dive of the Verde Island Passage and one of the most species-rich wall dives on Earth. The sheer vertical wall plunges from 3 m below the surface straight into the abyss, festooned with a continuous tapestry of soft corals, wire corals, sea fans, and crinoids in every colour. Current sweeping through the passage brings an endless procession of pelagics — dogtooth tuna, rainbow runners, and schools of jacks — while the wall itself shelters nudibranchs, mandarin fish, pygmy seahorses, and frogfish in the crevices. Scientists have recorded record fish species counts at this single site, making it arguably the most biodiverse marine location per square metre ever documented.
getThere: Verde Island is reached by bangka boat from Batangas City pier (approximately 45 minutes) or from Puerto Galera (approximately 30 minutes). Day trips depart daily from Anilao and Batangas. No accommodation on the island itself; divers stay in Batangas or Puerto Galera.

name: Sombrero Island
description: Sombrero Island, named for its distinctive hat shape, is surrounded by a fringing reef and a wall on its southern face that descends to 40 m. The site is celebrated for its dense schooling fish aggregations — vast tornadoes of glassfish (silversides) are regularly visited by hunting trevally, barracuda, and jacks that create dramatic feeding frenzies. The shallow reef top is a kaleidoscope of hard corals and anemone beds hosting clownfish, while the wall grows enormous sea fans and barrel sponges. Thresher sharks are occasionally sighted in the deeper blue water during the cooler months. The island also makes an excellent snorkel site in calm conditions.
getThere: Sombrero Island lies between Anilao and Verde Island. Bangka boats depart from Anilao (approximately 30 minutes) or Batangas City pier (approximately 50 minutes). Most Anilao dive resorts offer day trips.

name: Maricaban Island
description: Maricaban Island anchors the western edge of the Verde Island Passage and offers some of the area's finest macro diving alongside impressive wall topography. The island is surrounded by steep walls draped in black coral, sea fans, and a profusion of soft coral growth, while rubble and sand patches at the wall base shelter a remarkable array of small critters: flamboyant cuttlefish, robust ghost pipefish, Coleman shrimps, and multiple nudibranch species new to science have been found here. Seahorses are resident on the reef slope. Whale sharks pass through the passage seasonally, most reliably between November and February. The relative remoteness of Maricaban keeps dive traffic lower than Anilao's more accessible sites.
getThere: Maricaban Island is accessed by bangka boat from Anilao (approximately 40 minutes) or from Batangas City pier. Day trips are available from Anilao resorts; some operators also offer overnight liveaboard trips that include Maricaban in their itinerary.

name: Caban Point (Anilao)
description: Caban Point at Anilao is the gateway dive of the Verde Island Passage, where most divers first encounter the extraordinary biodiversity of this corridor. A rocky promontory creates converging currents that concentrate plankton and feeding fish, with the reef slope hosting a staggering density of small critters that has made Anilao synonymous with world-class macro photography. Hammerhead sharks patrol the blue water beyond the point in the cooler months, while the slope itself rewards patient photographers with painted frogfish, hairy frogfish, mimic octopus, blue-ringed octopus, and species of nudibranch encountered nowhere else. Hard coral recovery after bleaching events has been notable here, with resilient Acropora and Porites communities re-establishing in the shallows.
getThere: Anilao is approximately 2 hours by road south of Manila via the STAR toll road to Batangas, then a short drive to Anilao village. Bangka boats depart from the beach directly in front of the dive resorts. No domestic flights needed; most divers self-drive or take a bus from Manila.

name: Gili Tepekong
description: Gili Tepekong is a small rocky islet offshore from Candidasa with an underwater canyon system that channels strong currents and concentrates big pelagic life. White-tip reef sharks rest in the canyon, large schools of barracuda patrol the water column, and mola mola are occasionally spotted here in the season. The hard coral coverage on the walls is impressive, and the unpredictable currents make this a site best suited to experienced divers.
getThere: Boat from Candidasa harbour, approximately 20 minutes.

name: Gili Mimpang
description: Three rocky outcrops northeast of Candidasa form Gili Mimpang, an exciting drift and reef dive with sloping walls covered in sea fans and diverse soft corals. Black-tip and white-tip reef sharks are reliably seen here, along with large Napoleon wrasse and giant trevally hunting the reef edge. Current direction changes throughout the dive, keeping divers alert, and the nutrient-rich upwellings attract pelagic visitors regularly.
getThere: Boat from Candidasa harbour, approximately 25 minutes.

name: Gili Biaha
description: Gili Biaha is a small uninhabited island north of Candidasa known for its underwater cave and resident population of white-tip reef sharks. The cave entrance at around 15 metres leads into a shallow cavern where sharks rest during the day — one of the few accessible shark cave experiences in Bali. Outside the cave, walls drop to 30 metres with healthy hard coral and abundant reef fish. Strong currents are common so timing and briefing are essential.
getThere: Boat from Candidasa harbour, approximately 30 minutes.

name: Candidasa Reef
description: The fringing reef directly in front of Candidasa village provides an accessible shore and boat dive with coral gardens and sandy patches frequented by macro life. Nudibranchs, flatworms, pipefish, and frogfish are regularly found here, along with resident hawksbill turtles grazing on sponges. Large schools of barracuda are a signature of this site, gathering in the mid-water column. Conditions are gentler than the offshore gilis, making this a good option for less experienced divers or as a second dive.
getThere: Shore entry from Candidasa village beach, or short boat ride from local harbour.

name: Manta Point (Nusa Penida)
description: Manta Point on the south coast of Nusa Penida is one of the most reliable manta ray cleaning stations in Indonesia. Reef manta rays gather here year-round to be cleaned by wrasse at a series of cleaning stations along a sloping reef and rocky pinnacles. Divers descend to the reef and wait — the mantas often make multiple passes within arm's reach. Oceanic manta rays are occasionally recorded here too. Surge can be powerful on the exposed south coast so conditions require checking before diving.
getThere: Boat from Nusa Lembongan harbour, approximately 30 to 45 minutes around the south coast of Nusa Penida.

name: Crystal Bay
description: Crystal Bay on the northwest tip of Nusa Penida is the premier site for encountering oceanic sunfish (mola mola) in Bali. From July through October, mola mola rise from deep water to be cleaned at shallow reef areas, often appearing between 18 and 30 metres. The bay itself offers calmer conditions than the exposed south coast, with excellent hard coral coverage and a resident school of big-eye trevally. Cooler upwellings during peak mola season make a 5mm wetsuit essential.
getThere: Boat from Nusa Lembongan harbour, approximately 20 minutes to Crystal Bay on Nusa Penida's northwest coast.

name: SD Point
description: SD Point (named after a local school nearby) on Nusa Penida's northwest coast is a high-energy drift dive along a wall that drops to over 40 metres. Strong currents bring nutrients that feed an extraordinary density of marine life — vast schools of fusiliers and jacks attract tuna and barracuda, while white-tip and black-tip reef sharks cruise the wall edge. The hard coral coverage is among the best in the area. This site is for experienced drift divers only given the powerful and sometimes unpredictable currents.
getThere: Boat from Nusa Lembongan harbour, approximately 15 minutes to the northwest coast of Nusa Penida.

name: Toyapakeh
description: Toyapakeh is a diverse drift dive in the channel between Nusa Penida and Nusa Ceningan, offering a sloping reef with hard corals, sea fans, and an impressive diversity of reef fish. The site is well known for large schools of bumphead parrotfish that graze across the reef in groups of up to 50 individuals. Reef manta rays pass through the channel on feeding runs and Napoleon wrasse are common. Current strength varies considerably with tide, and the drift can push divers gently or powerfully depending on timing.
getThere: Boat from Nusa Lembongan harbour, approximately 10 minutes across the channel to Toyapakeh on Nusa Penida.

name: Bowen Island
description: The rocky reef circling Bowen Island is the signature dive of Jervis Bay Marine Park and a reliable address for wobbegong sharks. Spotted, banded and tasselled wobbegongs drape themselves over ledges and boulders at every depth from 5 to 20 metres, sometimes stacked on top of one another. Eastern blue groper, large schools of luderick and yellowtail scad move through in dense formations, while Port Jackson sharks rest in crevices from June through October. Visibility is exceptional year-round thanks to the near-pristine catchment feeding the bay.
getThere: Shore dive from Greenfield Beach or boat charter from Huskisson Wharf, approximately 10 minutes by boat.

name: The Docks
description: A shallow ledge system on the northern side of Jervis Bay that shelters one of the bay's most accessible grey nurse shark aggregation sites. Between June and November, several nurse sharks typically rest in the deeper gutters between 18 and 22 metres while the shallower ledge tops are carpeted in sponge gardens. The protected calm conditions here make it the preferred site when swell closes down the more exposed southern sites. Nudibranchs are prolific in the shallows, and eastern fiddler rays are common on the sand patches.
getThere: Boat dive only, approximately 15 minutes from Huskisson Wharf. Most local operators include this site in their daily two-tank itineraries.

name: Bush Bay
description: Bush Bay's shallow rocky reef on the western shore of Jervis Bay is one of the best muck and macro sites in southern New South Wales. Weedy seadragons are resident year-round here, often sighted on the kelp margins at 8 to 12 metres. Decorator crabs, seahorses and an impressive diversity of nudibranchs reward patient searching. When manta rays move into the bay between November and March they regularly pass through Bush Bay's shallower margins, making it one of the few manta sites that is also genuinely good for photographers spending time at depth.
getThere: Shore dive accessible from the bush track off Plantation Point Road, or boat charter from Huskisson. Boat is preferred for the outer reef sections.

name: Manta Lodge Wall
description: A dramatic sandstone wall dropping from 8 metres to 28 metres on the eastern side of Jervis Bay, named for the regular manta ray sightings that cluster near the wall in late spring and summer. The wall face is encrusted in orange and purple sponge colonies with large plate and fan corals on the deeper sections. Wobbegong sharks are tucked into nearly every horizontal surface on the wall, while large cephalopods including giant cuttlefish emerge after dark. The site is exposed to easterly swell and is best dived in settled autumn and spring conditions.
getThere: Boat only from Huskisson or Vincentia boat ramps, approximately 20 minutes. Sheltered anchorage on the northern end of the wall. Not accessible in easterly swells above 1 metre.

name: Julian Rocks North
description: The northern face of Julian Rocks (Nguthungulli) drops steeply from 5 metres to about 22 metres and is where the tropical influence of the East Australian Current is most apparent. Leopard sharks and tawny nurse sharks rest on the sand below the wall in summer alongside wobegongs and shovel-nosed rays. This face sees more surge than the south side but also stronger fish aggregations, with large schools of yellowtail scad, trevally and fusiliers moving in columns around the pinnacle. Manta rays frequently cruise the north wall during their March to May transit.
getThere: Boat dive only, 10 to 15 minutes from Byron Bay boat ramp at Jonson Street. All local operators use the same ramp; book direct to confirm morning departure times.

name: Julian Rocks South
description: The southern and more sheltered face of Julian Rocks is where grey nurse sharks (critically endangered in Australia) aggregate in winter, resting in the rocky gutters between 15 and 22 metres. Up to 30 individuals have been recorded at one time during peak aggregation season from June through September, making this one of only a handful of reliable grey nurse aggregation sites on the east coast. The calmer conditions here suit less experienced divers and provide a more stable platform for photography. Wobbegong sharks, large green turtles and eagle rays are year-round residents.
getThere: Boat dive from Byron Bay boat ramp, 10 to 15 minutes. Operators moor on the south side mooring buoys. Marine park zone B regulations apply — no taking of marine life.

name: The Nursery
description: A flat sandy gutter system on the eastern side of Julian Rocks that acts as a sheltered resting habitat for juvenile and subadult grey nurse sharks during their winter aggregation. The gutters run at 16 to 20 metres, with a sandy floor and boulders providing shelter. The site gets its name from the proportion of smaller individuals — juveniles and sub-adults that congregate here while older adults rest in the main southern gutter. Eagle rays and shovelnose rays are regular company on the sand. Conditions are generally calmer than the main site faces, making it well suited to early-stage open water divers.
getThere: Boat only from Byron Bay boat ramp, approximately 15 minutes. Most operators combine this with a second site at Julian Rocks main on the same boat trip.

name: Cook Island
description: Cook Island Aquatic Reserve sits just south of the Queensland border and north of Byron Bay, accessible from Fingal Head. The island's rocky reef system holds some of the highest coral cover on this stretch of coast, with hard coral gardens on the northern faces in 10 to 20 metres. Common dolphins regularly pass through on early morning boat trips and occasionally interact with divers in the water. Green turtles are abundant and among the most relaxed in the region — resting under ledges and feeding on algae with little concern for divers. Reef fish diversity is notably higher here than at Julian Rocks, reflecting the stronger tropical influence.
getThere: Boat from Fingal Head boat ramp, approximately 10 minutes, or from Byron Bay via some operators offering the combined trip. Shore entries are possible on very calm days from the island's eastern side.

name: Shell Beach Reef
description: A shallow reef system adjacent to the world-famous Shell Beach, composed almost entirely of cockle shells in the hypersal L'Haridon Bight. Divers encounter dense seagrass beds hosting juvenile fish, sea snakes, loggerhead turtles, and occasional tiger sharks cruising the sandy margins. The combination of high salinity and warm shallows produces unusual invertebrate assemblages rarely seen elsewhere.
getThere: Access by boat from Denham, the main town in Shark Bay, approximately 30 minutes by vessel.

name: Dirk Hartog Island Wall
description: The western face of Dirk Hartog Island — the largest island in Western Australia — drops away in a series of ledges and undercuts frequented by wobbegong sharks, large snapper, and schools of trevally. Tiger sharks are a regular presence, as are loggerhead and green turtles. The site is exposed to Indian Ocean swells, which concentrates nutrients and drives excellent pelagic activity along the wall.
getThere: Liveaboard or charter vessel from Denham. Dirk Hartog Island is approximately 60 km by sea. Day trips are weather-dependent.

name: Monkey Mia Seagrass Flats
description: The vast Wooramel Seagrass Bank — the largest in the world — spreads across these shallows near the famous Monkey Mia dolphin beach. Snorkellers and divers explore meadows hosting hundreds of dugongs feeding on Amphibolis and Posidonia. Tiger sharks shadow the herds with the regularity documented in the Shark Bay Ecosystem Research Project. Depth is slight but the density of megafauna is extraordinary.
getThere: Short boat ride from Monkey Mia Resort jetty, or shore access from the Monkey Mia beach area. Denham is 26 km to the south.

name: Francois Peron Bommies
description: Scattered coral bommies off the Francois Peron National Park coastline provide structure in an otherwise flat bay environment. Resident reef fish, octopus, and moray eels colonise the heads, which also attract hunting tiger sharks and large stingrays. The red-ochre cliffs of the peninsula form a dramatic backdrop above the surface while the bommies below hold some of the bay's most concentrated fish life.
getThere: Boat access from Denham, approximately 20 to 40 minutes depending on destination bommie. 4WD access to Francois Peron NP from Denham for shore-based exploration.

name: Direction Island Drift
description: The northern tip of Direction Island funnels Indian Ocean currents through a shallow passage, creating one of the atoll's most exhilarating drift dives. Scalloped hammerheads, grey reef sharks, and silvertip sharks patrol the current seam while schools of bigeye trevally and fusiliers sweep past in dense columns. Coral coverage on the shallow plateau is among the best-preserved in the territory.
getThere: Fly to Cocos (Keeling) Islands Airport (CCK) via Perth on Virgin Australia. Boat transfers to dive sites arranged through the island's dive operator or liveaboard.

name: Shark's Gut
description: A deep channel cutting through the western reef brings open-ocean species into contact with the atoll structure. Silvertip sharks and grey reef sharks are resident, hammerheads appear regularly at depth, and occasional whale sharks pass through on the surface. The channel walls are draped in sea fans and black coral from 20 m down, with strong currents delivering plankton and the larger animals that feed on them.
getThere: Boat from Home Island or West Island. Strong current timing makes morning slack-water entry preferable. Advanced diver experience recommended.

name: Prison Island Wall
description: The southern lagoon wall near the historic Prison Island drops sharply from the reef flat into deep water, sheltering a diverse community of reef fish alongside steady shark traffic. The wall is notably colourful with encrusting sponges and soft corals, and resident turtles rest in the larger cavities. This is one of the more sheltered sites in the atoll and accessible in moderate wind conditions when exposed reef edges are unusable.
getThere: Short boat ride from Home Island jetty. One of the most accessible dive sites in the territory and a good first dive for orientation to the atoll.

name: Horseshoe
description: A horseshoe-shaped reef formation on the northern atoll rim creates a natural amphitheatre where currents eddy and concentrate marine life. Manta rays cruise the cleaning stations here with regularity during April through September, joined by eagle rays and the ever-present grey reef and blacktip sharks. The reef crest is extraordinarily healthy, with almost no bleaching visible in recent years, and the drop-off delivers walls of anthias and glassfish.
getThere: Boat from Home Island or Direction Island, approximately 15 to 25 minutes. Current windows determine entry timing — check locally on arrival.

name: The Wall
description: Osezaki's signature wall plunges from 6 metres at the surface to beyond 40 metres, its face carpeted in dense colonies of soft coral in orange, white, and purple. The nutrient current sweeping up from the deep basin of Suruga Bay sustains the coral growth and draws enormous schools of yellowtail fusiliers that orbit the wall face throughout the day. Large grouper and moray eels occupy the crevices, and the wall's upper lip hosts some of Izu's most vibrant encrusting invertebrate communities. Best dived on the incoming tide when visibility opens up and the school density is highest.
getThere: Osezaki is accessible from Numazu or Mishima Station (JR Tokaido Line), then bus or taxi to Osezaki dive services on the cape. Most divers shore-enter from the designated dive area managed by local operators.

name: Shark Ledge
description: A series of broad sand and rubble ledges between 20 and 30 metres where whitetip reef sharks gather to rest during daylight hours, often lying motionless in groups of three to six individuals beneath overhangs. The sharks are habituated to divers and allow close approach, making this one of the most reliable shark encounters in Japan. The surrounding reef is characterised by large boulder formations with crevices hosting lionfish, scorpionfish, and juvenile moray eels. At dusk the sharks become active and hunt the reef alongside banded sea kraits.
getThere: Reach Osezaki by bus or taxi from Numazu Station. Shark Ledge is a boat dive from Osezaki port, approximately 5 minutes from the launch point. Local dive operators run scheduled daily boats.

name: Fusilier Reef
description: A broad sloping reef from 8 to 28 metres where Suruga Bay's productive currents concentrate enormous schools of yellowtail fusiliers that at peak season number in the tens of thousands. The school forms a shimmering curtain that divers can enter, surrounded by fish on all sides, while yellowfin tuna and amberjack patrol the school's periphery making high-speed predatory runs. The reef base hosts encrusting sponges, sea fans, and occasional octopus in the rubble. This is the best site for wide-angle photography when the school is thick, typically April through June and September through November.
getThere: Boat dive from Osezaki port. Operators depart from the small harbour adjacent to the shore dive entry area. The site is 5 to 8 minutes by boat from shore.

name: Deep Pinnacle
description: An isolated volcanic pinnacle rising from 45 metres to a summit at 22 metres, its flanks densely covered in large gorgonian sea fans and black coral trees that thrive in the consistent cold upwelling from Suruga Bay's deep basin. The pinnacle acts as a cleaning station and aggregation point — schools of large amberjack and striped bonito orbit the structure, while scorpionfish and anglerfish occupy the rubble and coralline algae at the base. Hammerhead sharks pass through on seasonal migrations from April to June. This is an advanced dive requiring solid buoyancy control and experience with moderate current.
getThere: Advanced boat dive from Osezaki port, approximately 10 minutes from shore. Dive operators run this site on days with appropriate conditions. Minimum certification recommended: Advanced Open Water with deep dive speciality.

name: Tsurigasaki
description: Tsurigasaki is the flagship nudibranch site of Sagami Bay, a broad rocky reef from 5 to 20 metres colonised by dozens of hydroid and bryozoan species that in turn support extraordinary nudibranch densities. Local guides tally over 80 nudibranch species at this single site, including cold-water specialists like Flabellina, Trinchesia, and Cuthona genera that require water below 18 degrees Celsius. Wobbegong sharks rest wedged into crevices along the reef base, and juvenile cuttlefish aggregate in the kelp fronds from March through May. Visibility is best in winter when plankton blooms subside and the cold water stratifies cleanly.
getThere: Tateyama is 2.5 hours from Tokyo via the Uchibo Line from Soga Station. Tsurigasaki is a short drive or taxi from Tateyama Station. Several local dive shops in Tateyama operate boat and shore dives to this site.

name: Hamasakishita
description: Hamasakishita is a sheltered shore dive site on the Tateyama waterfront, a gently sloping sand and rubble bottom from 3 to 18 metres that functions as prime nursery habitat for juvenile fish and invertebrates. The site is renowned for the density and variety of frogfish species found on sponges and encrusted boulders across the shallows, with painted, warty, and hairy frogfish all recorded in a single dive on good days. Ghost pipefish appear seasonally in the seagrass patches, and the night dive reveals an entirely different community including spider crabs, flatworms, and feeding cephalopods. The sheltered bay position makes this a reliable dive in almost any weather.
getThere: Shore entry from Tateyama town waterfront. Dive centres in Tateyama can arrange guided shore dives with equipment rental. The entry point is within walking distance of several dive shops on the harbourfront.

name: Jogashima
description: Jogashima Island at the mouth of Sagami Bay marks the transition between the sheltered inner bay and the open Pacific, producing a unique mix of temperate reef species and seasonal pelagic visitors. The rocky reef from 8 to 30 metres is heavily colonised by encrusting red and pink coralline algae, with dense populations of nudibranchs, especially Tritonia, Dendronotus, and large dorids in winter. The stronger currents here compared to inner bay sites bring schools of horse mackerel and yellowtail amberjack, and the occasional blue shark passes by in late summer. Wobbegong sharks are a consistent highlight, wedged into rock shelves at 12 to 18 metres year-round.
getThere: Jogashima Island is reached via Keikyu Misakiguchi Station on the Keikyu Kurihama Line from Yokohama (about 60 minutes), then bus to Jogashima. Dive operators in Misaki town run regular boat charters to the island's dive sites.

name: Moroiso
description: Moroiso on the Miura Peninsula is one of Japan's most data-rich cold-water macro sites, with local dive clubs maintaining species lists exceeding 130 nudibranch species across multiple decades of records. The site consists of a gentle rocky slope from 5 to 22 metres with extensive coralline algae mats, kelp fronds, and hydroid colonies that provide habitat complexity for some of Japan's rarest seaslugs. Japanese wobbegong sharks — a species endemic to Japanese and Korean waters — are a signature animal here, resting in shallow rock gullies at 8 to 12 metres and rarely disturbed by patient divers. Winter brings the best nudibranch diversity as cold water suppresses visibility-reducing plankton and triggers breeding aggregations.
getThere: Moroiso is on the Miura Peninsula, reached via Keikyu Misaki-guchi Station and then a 10 minute taxi to the dive area. Multiple dive shops operate from Moroiso harbour with shore dive access and boat options.

name: Manta Cleaning Station
description: The most reliable manta ray encounter in Palau — a sandy-bottomed cleaning station inside the German Channel where resident oceanic manta rays queue up to be groomed by cleaner wrasse and butterflyfish. Divers kneel on the sand or hold a coral ridge while mantas glide overhead in slow, banking circuits, sometimes within arm's reach. Multiple rays often visit simultaneously, and on strong incoming tides the channel current concentrates plankton that draws additional pelagics including eagle rays and reef sharks.
getThere: Depart by boat from Koror or Malakal Harbor — approximately 45 minutes by speedboat. Most dive operators in Koror run dedicated German Channel manta trips with two to three dives, timed to coincide with incoming tides when manta activity peaks.

name: Shark City
description: A dramatic wall and plateau site just south of German Channel where grey reef sharks and whitetip reef sharks congregate in numbers that justify the name. The outer wall drops past 40 meters with strong currents that aggregate fish life and nutrients, drawing sharks into a visible mass on the reef edge. Bumphead parrotfish schools are a morning feature, and the plateau top at 15 meters is one of Palau's most productive shark-watching perches.
getThere: Reached by boat from Koror in approximately 40 minutes. Best dived on an incoming tide when currents push nutrient-rich water up the wall, concentrating shark activity. Hook deployment is standard practice on the plateau edge.

name: Turtle Cove
description: A sheltered bay on the eastern edge of the German Channel approach where green and hawksbill turtles rest and feed on sponge-encrusted rock. The calm conditions make this a reliable second dive site after the manta station, with excellent macro life in the seagrass and rubble zones including ornate ghost pipefish, flamboyant cuttlefish, and blue-ringed octopus. Nudibranchs and flatworms cover every surface in remarkable variety.
getThere: A short boat ride from the German Channel manta station, typically included as a second dive on German Channel day trips from Koror. The calm, shallow conditions make it accessible for all certification levels.

name: West Passage Wall
description: A sweeping vertical wall on the western approach to German Channel that drops from 10 meters to beyond recreational limits, draped in enormous sea fans, black coral trees, and barrel sponges. The wall faces open ocean and intercepts strong tidal currents, making it one of the most productive pelagic corridors in Palau. Oceanic whitetip sharks are occasional visitors, and grey reef sharks patrol the wall edge in the permanent thermocline where warm surface water meets the cooler oceanic column.
getThere: Accessed by boat from Koror, approximately 50 minutes. Dive operators time entries to use the current rather than fight it — the standard approach is a drift along the wall face, surfacing at a pre-arranged pick-up point down-current.

name: USS Apogon
description: The USS Apogon is a Tench-class submarine sunk during Operation Crossroads, now resting upright on the lagoon floor at 50 meters — one of only a handful of diveable submarines in the world. She sits intact with her conning tower rising to 38 meters, her torpedo tubes still loaded and open, and her interior accessible to technical divers through hatches that remain open after 80 years on the bottom. The compressed scale of a submarine makes every centimeter alive with encrusting coral, sponge, and the surreal juxtaposition of wartime hardware draped in tropical reef.
getThere: Access requires a liveaboard expedition to Bikini Atoll — the nearest regular flights land on Majuro or Kwajalein, followed by a charter flight to Bikini. The atoll has no permanent dive infrastructure; all diving is conducted from the liveaboard vessel. Advance booking with a specialist Bikini liveaboard operator is essential.

name: Parcel das Paredes
description: An offshore pinnacle system rising from 30 m to within 8 m of the surface at the entrance to Todos os Santos Bay. Strong seasonal upwellings bring whale sharks between July and November. The walls are draped in encrusting sponges and black coral with large schools of Atlantic spadefish and horse-eye jacks circling the summit.
getThere: Boat dive departing from the Marina Bahia or Ilha de Maré; approximately 45 minutes by fast boat from Salvador city centre.

name: Pedra de Lixa
description: A shallow rocky reef system inside Todos os Santos Bay, famous for resident longsnout seahorses, robust ghost pipefish, and a remarkable diversity of nudibranchs sheltering in the rubble and soft-coral patches. Visibility is moderate but rewarding for macro photographers willing to move slowly.
getThere: Short boat transfer from the Comércio waterfront or Ribeira pier; most Salvador dive operators run day trips here.

name: Ilha dos Frades Norte
description: The northern tip of Ilha dos Frades offers clear bay waters with coral heads populated by parrotfish, triggerfish, and green moray eels. Hawksbill turtles are reliably sighted grazing on sponges, and the sandy channels between coral bommies attract spotted eagle rays on incoming tides.
getThere: Boat from Salvador; Ilha dos Frades is roughly 25 minutes by fast boat from Ribeira or the Terminal Náutico.

name: Recife de Fora de Itapuã
description: An outer reef barrier running parallel to the Itapuã coast, exposed enough to attract pelagic species yet accessible for recreational divers. Reef sharks patrol the deeper seaward edge while the lagoon-side slopes hold dense coral gardens with Caribbean-style butterfly fish, angelfish, and abundant sergeant majors.
getThere: Boat from Itapuã beach or Stella Maris; approximately 20 minutes to the reef edge; day trips run from several Salvador dive centres.

name: Caverna da Freira
description: A granite cavern system on the northwestern coast of Ilha Grande where light plays through cracks in the rock to illuminate colonies of encrusting red and purple sponges. The cavern ceiling hosts a dense population of glass shrimp and the entrance is frequented by green turtles resting on the sandy bottom.
getThere: Boat from Vila do Abraão, the main village on Ilha Grande; approximately 20 minutes by dive tender to the northwest coast.

name: Pedra d'Água
description: A submerged granite pinnacle rising from 25 m to 4 m depth on the south coast, swept by the cold thermocline currents of the Atlantic. Endemic species including the Brazilian grunt and colourful Brazilian basslet are common, and the hard current brings good visibility and healthy soft-coral growth across the rock faces.
getThere: Boat from Vila do Abraão; approximately 35 minutes around the southern tip of the island; check current forecasts before departure as the site can be diveable only on slack tide.

name: Navio Grécia Wreck
description: A small coastal freighter resting upright in 18 to 24 m on a sandy bottom near the protected eastern bay. Penetration-friendly for recreational divers with good torches, the interior has been colonised by batfish, glassy sweepers, and large groupers. The hull exterior hosts encrusting hydroids and is cleaned by battalions of cleaner shrimp.
getThere: Short boat transfer from Vila do Abraão; approximately 10 minutes; most local dive operators include this site on their standard day-trip roster.

name: Ponta do Leste
description: The easternmost tip of Ilha Grande where Atlantic Ocean swells create a mild drift along a stepped granite wall dropping to 30 m. Green and hawksbill turtles are reliably present, endemic Brazilian reef fish school in the upper zones, and the deeper ledges shelter jewfish grouper and large southern stingrays resting on sandy patches.
getThere: Boat from Vila do Abraão; approximately 40 minutes to the eastern tip; best dived on mild swell days as ocean exposure can make entry difficult.

name: Pedra de Galé
description: A dramatic volcanic pinnacle rising from 40 m to just below the surface on the southwest coast of Príncipe. The seamount is encrusted with black coral, large sea fans, and sponges, and attracts impressive aggregations of jacks, barracuda, and snapper. Whale sharks are sighted here during the boreal summer months, and oceanic triggerfish circle the peak in large schools. The site demands solid buoyancy control due to upwellings and moderate current.
getThere: Príncipe is reached via São Tomé International Airport with onward flights to Príncipe Airport (STP to PCP). The island has one dedicated dive operator, HBD Príncipe, based at the Bom Bom Island Resort. All dive logistics depart from the resort's jetty.

name: Ilhéu Bom Bom
description: The small islet adjacent to Bom Bom resort creates a sheltered channel dive accessible to all levels. Soft corals, wire coral, and juvenile reef fish crowd the rocky walls that slope from 3 m down to 25 m. Moray eels, porcupinefish, and hawksbill turtles are resident year-round. Because the site is close to the main jetty it works perfectly as a night dive, when octopus, cuttlefish, and bioluminescent plankton are consistently encountered.
getThere: Príncipe is reached via São Tomé International Airport with onward flights to Príncipe Airport. Ilhéu Bom Bom is a 5-minute boat ride from the Bom Bom Island Resort jetty and is the resort's house reef.

name: Sete Pedras
description: Seven volcanic boulders scattered across a sandy plateau on the southeast coast create a distinctive dive site with exceptional macro life and good fish density. The gaps between the boulders shelter nudibranchs, frogfish, and cleaning stations attended by endemic Príncipe sunbird wrasse. Larger boulders are coated in encrusting sponge and cup coral. A reliable hammerhead cleaning station sits at 28 m on the outer edge, active primarily in the dry season.
getThere: Accessed by boat from Bom Bom Island Resort, approximately 25 minutes by dive tender. Best visited on a day trip with the resort's dive operation. Surface conditions can be choppy from July through September.

name: Banana Beach Wall
description: A vertical wall beginning at 6 m and dropping beyond 40 m on the northwest coast, within swimming distance of Príncipe's most famous beach. The wall face is covered in black coral trees and large orange and yellow barrel sponges. Pygmy seahorses have been documented on sea fans here, and the resident population of green turtles is unusually dense. Upwellings from the wall bring occasional manta rays and eagle rays into the blue water off the face.
getThere: A short boat ride of roughly 15 minutes from Bom Bom Island Resort. Snorkel entry is technically possible from Banana Beach itself, though the wall is best reached by dinghy to ensure proper descent point positioning.

name: Jardin des Coraux
description: A sprawling coral garden inside the inner lagoon with exceptional hard coral cover including table Acropora, brain coral, and massive Porites heads up to 3 m across. The calm, shallow conditions make this a superb site for underwater photography and for spotting the lagoon's resident dugong population — Mayotte hosts one of the largest dugong groups in the western Indian Ocean. Green and hawksbill turtles graze the seagrass beds adjacent to the coral formations.
getThere: Located inside the inner lagoon, accessible by boat from Mamoudzou in approximately 20 minutes. Several dive operators run morning sessions timed around optimal light for photography. Entry via shore is possible from certain points on Petite Terre.

name: La Vigie
description: A prominent coral pinnacle on the eastern inner lagoon that acts as a cleaning station for large pelagics. Whale sharks are sighted here year-round, most frequently between October and March. The pinnacle tops out at 5 m and its base spreads to 30 m, with whip corals, sea fans, and an impressive concentration of barracuda. Manta rays visit the cleaning station on the pinnacle top, hovering while cleaner wrasse attend them — one of the most reliably observed manta encounters in the western Indian Ocean.
getThere: Reached by boat from Mamoudzou or Bandraboua in 30 to 45 minutes depending on departure point. Dive operators typically combine La Vigie with a second site on the eastern reef for a full day trip.

name: Banc du Choizil
description: A submerged reef bank in the northern lagoon that rises from 35 m to a broad plateau at 12 m. From July through September humpback whale mothers and calves rest in the calm water above the plateau, and snorkeling or freediving encounters are conducted here under strict no-scuba protocols to avoid disturbing the animals. SCUBA divers explore the walls and undercuts of the bank, which are home to nurse sharks, large grouper, and schools of batfish. The site represents one of the few places in the world where humpback whale acoustic encounters are reliably experienced underwater.
getThere: A 50 to 60 minute boat ride from Mamoudzou into the northern lagoon. Access is managed by local dive operators who coordinate with Mayotte marine park authorities for humpback season protocols (July to September). Outside whale season the site is a straightforward SCUBA destination.

name: Saltö Wall
description: A near-vertical granite wall on the southern tip of Saltö island drops from 2 metres to beyond 40 metres. The surface is smothered in dead man's fingers soft coral, plumose anemones, and encrusting sponges in orange and yellow. Nudibranchs are the headline attraction — Flabellina nobilis, Onchidoris muricata, and Limacia clavigera appear on virtually every dive. Sea spiders with leg-spans approaching 10 centimetres cling to the sponge fields. Visibility in the national park is consistently high, making the wall's colour and texture unmissable.
getThere: Take the ferry from Strömstad to Sydkoster island, then arrange a shore entry or boat charter from Kosterhavet's local dive operators. Strömstad is 1.5 hours by car north of Gothenburg.

name: Koster Trench
description: The Koster Trench is the northern extension of the Norwegian Trench and the deepest point in Swedish waters at over 240 metres. Technical and advanced recreational divers descend the upper reaches of this submarine canyon to witness a deep-sea community rarely seen at accessible depths: stalked crinoids, large spider crabs, Norway lobster (langoustine) emerging from burrows, and at the shallower edges, dense horse mussel beds that host entire micro-ecosystems. The cold, oxygen-rich water produces exceptional clarity — a defining feature of Kosterhavet National Park.
getThere: Boat dive only — depart from Strömstad or Koster island with a technical dive charter. Advanced buoyancy and cold-water experience required. Gas planning essential given depth.

name: Stängselrevet Reef
description: Stängselrevet is a shallow rocky reef system running parallel to the Koster coastline, protected within the national park boundaries. Kelp forests of sugar kelp and oarweed dominate the upper 8 metres, giving way to open rock encrusted with soft corals and sponges. This is one of the best sites in Sweden to observe the full range of Kosterfjord's macro life in a single dive: leopard-spotted nudibranchs, painted gobies hiding in mussel clusters, and large common lobsters wedged into crevices. Shore entry is possible, making it ideal for independent divers staying on Koster island.
getThere: Shore entry from Sydkoster island. Walk the marked coastal path from the ferry dock at Ekenäs, approximately 20 minutes. The entry point is signposted within the national park.

name: Nordkoster Urchin Fields
description: The northern tip of Nordkoster island is where the Kosterfjord current meets the open Skagerrak, creating ideal conditions for filter-feeding communities. Dense carpets of green sea urchins cover the bedrock from 5 metres down, and their grazing creates openings colonised by tunicates, bryozoans, and the brilliantly coloured Coryphella nudibranchs that feed on them. Edible crabs and velvet swimming crabs are abundant in the crevices. The site experiences stronger tidal movement than the sheltered southern sites, which brings nutrients but requires careful timing — slack water dives are the most productive.
getThere: Boat or kayak from Nordkoster harbour. Check tide tables and plan for slack water — the site becomes a strong drift dive on a running tide. Local dive shops in Strömstad can advise on timing.

name: Lysefjord Wall
description: The inner Lysefjord wall is where the granite cliff that rises to Preikestolen above continues straight down below the surface. The wall is blanketed in dead man's fingers soft corals — white and orange colonies stacked on every ledge — interspersed with large plumose anemones and cup corals. Wolf fish occupy the deeper overhangs, often resting in pairs. The absence of boat traffic and the sheltered nature of the inner fjord keep the water very calm, and the cliff walls block wind, making this one of Norway's most accessible cold-water wall dives despite its remote appearance.
getThere: Drive from Stavanger to Forsand at the mouth of Lysefjord (40 minutes), or take the Lysefjord boat tour and arrange a dive charter. Several Stavanger dive clubs run organised Lysefjord trips in summer.

name: Preikestolen Drop
description: Directly below Preikestolen (Pulpit Rock), the fjord floor is 422 metres below the famous cliff ledge. The dive site works the upper section of this sheer underwater cliff face, which mirrors the vertical drama above the surface. Visibility is at its peak here in winter and early spring when cold freshwater melt is minimal, and the depth provides a thermocline-free dive in high summer. Juvenile wolffish are regularly spotted sheltering in crevices along the wall, and the density of Metridium anemones — standing 30 to 40 centimetres tall — is among the highest recorded in any Norwegian fjord.
getThere: Boat only — depart from Forsand or Lauvvik on the northern shore. The site is 25 minutes by RIB from Forsand. No shore access exists at this point of the fjord due to vertical cliffs.

name: Stavanger Harbour Wrecks
description: The approaches to Stavanger harbour contain several accessible wrecks from World War II and the early oil era, sitting in 18 to 35 metres. The most visited is a fishing vessel resting upright on a sandy bottom, its hull now encrusted with soft corals and mussels. Visibility is lower than the open fjord but the wreck offers a controlled environment for exploring cabins, holds, and the propeller, all colonised by nudibranchs and gobies. Atlantic cod hover around the bow in large numbers, and the wrecks attract Norway's characteristic cold-water sponge life that transforms metal into a living reef over decades.
getThere: Boat charter from Stavanger city marina. Multiple local dive clubs and operators run regular wreck trips. City centre Stavanger has good transport links — Stavanger Airport connects to Oslo and international hubs.

name: Sandnes Macro Reef
description: The sheltered waters of Gandsfjord between Stavanger and Sandnes host a series of rocky reef systems that are largely unknown outside Norwegian diving communities. The reefs sit in 6 to 28 metres and are blanketed in sponge and bryozoan communities that support an extraordinary density of dorid nudibranchs. This is one of the best sites in Norway specifically for photography — calm conditions, short boat ride, and subjects that stay still. Lumpsucker fish appear in late winter and early spring to breed, attaching their egg masses to rocks in the shallows in a display rarely witnessed by divers at most European sites.
getThere: Short boat ride from Sandnes marina, 20 minutes south of Stavanger by car or local bus. Sandnes Dykkerklubb runs regular club dives at this site and welcomes visiting divers with prior arrangement.

name: Sunken Cemetery
description: One of the Philippines' most iconic dive sites, the Sunken Cemetery marks where an 1871 volcanic eruption submerged a coastal village and its graveyard beneath the sea. A large white cross on the surface marks the spot, and beneath it coral-encrusted headstones and rubble spread across a sloping reef from 3 to 18 metres. Lionfish and scorpionfish rest among the coral heads, moorish idols and butterflyfish move in loose pairs, and the occasional guitar shark rests on sand patches at depth. The combination of dramatic historical context and genuine coral health makes this one of the most memorable easy dives in Mindanao.
getThere: Dive operators in Mambajao town, the island capital, run daily trips by banca. The site is approximately 10 minutes offshore from the town wharf.

name: Mantigue Island Marine Sanctuary
description: Mantigue Island is a small coral atoll to the northeast of Camiguin protected as a marine sanctuary, and the protection shows in the reef condition. Hard coral cover is dense and largely intact, with table corals, staghorn colonies, and brain corals in sizes rarely seen in unprotected areas. Sea turtles — both green and hawksbill — are resident and approachable. The sandy seagrass patches between the reef and the beach are consistent hunting grounds for blue-spotted ribbontail rays. The shallow plateau at 6 to 12 metres is ideal for multiple dives per day, and the outer slope drops to 25 metres along a wall that supports schools of fusiliers and hunting trevally.
getThere: Bancas depart from Benoni Port on the northeast coast of Camiguin. The crossing takes approximately 20 minutes. Dive operators in Mambajao organise combined banca and guide packages.

name: Jigdup Reef
description: Jigdup Reef sits off the western shore of Camiguin and is the island's premier wall dive, a vertical drop from 5 metres to beyond 40 that is carpeted in sea fans, black coral trees, and massive sponges. Strong upwellings from the deeper water regularly push nutrient-rich cold patches through the site, which draws grey reef sharks, dogtooth tuna, and large schools of big-eye trevally. Whale sharks are occasionally sighted in the channel between Camiguin and the mainland from November through April. The topside volcanic scenery — Hibok-Hibok and four other volcanic peaks visible above the tree line — adds a dimension that few dive sites can match.
getThere: A 15 minute banca ride from dive resorts on the western coast of Camiguin near Guinsiliban. Most operators run the site as a drift dive, timing the entry to the current direction.

name: White Island Channel
description: The shallow sandbar of White Island creates a natural channel between the island and Camiguin's northern shore, and the tidal flow through this gap concentrates fish and marine life in volumes that surprise first-time visitors. The seafloor here is a mix of black volcanic sand, rubble, and healthy coral patches — classic muck diving territory. Thorough searching rewards divers with flamboyant cuttlefish, frogfish in multiple colour morphs, harlequin ghost pipefish, and a rotating cast of nudibranchs. The site suits all levels and doubles as an excellent night dive when the bioluminescent plankton activates after dark.
getThere: Accessible by banca from resorts along Camiguin's north coast near Agoho. The crossing to White Island takes 5 minutes; divers enter the channel from the Camiguin side.

name: Sardine Wall
description: The western face of Pescador Island is where the sardine run — one of the most photographed phenomena in Philippine diving — unfolds. Millions of sardines move in tight bait balls that twist and contract against the wall in response to the hunting passes of thresher sharks, jacks, and rainbow runners. The curtain of fish can be so dense it blocks ambient light, creating an otherworldly silver tunnel around divers who position themselves at mid-water. The wall itself drops from 3 metres to beyond 35, with sea fans and black coral providing structure for pygmy seahorses and ghost pipefish. The sardine aggregation peaks between March and June but is present year-round in smaller numbers.
getThere: Bancas depart from Panagsama Beach in Moalboal, southwest Cebu. The crossing to Pescador Island takes 15 to 20 minutes. Dozens of dive operators on Panagsama Beach offer multiple daily trips.

name: Cathedral Cave
description: Cathedral Cave is a large cavern on the north face of Pescador Island where a collapsed ceiling has created a shaft that funnels sunlight down into the chamber in a single dramatic beam — the phenomenon that gives the site its name. At the right time of day the light column illuminates clouds of glassfish suspended in the cave mouth while silvertip bats roost in the dry upper sections. Moray eels of several species occupy the crevices at the entrance, and lionfish hang motionless in the shadows. The cavern extends to around 18 metres and opens back to the wall outside. Divers with no cavern certification should stay within the light zone; the restrictions are clearly defined and the site rewards the discipline.
getThere: Accessed by banca from Panagsama Beach, Moalboal. Most operators combine Cathedral Cave with the Sardine Wall as a two-dive trip on the same boat. Torches recommended even for the entrance chamber.

name: North Pinnacle
description: The North Pinnacle is a submerged rock pillar that rises from 35 metres to within 8 metres of the surface off the northern tip of Pescador. Current funnels around the pinnacle and creates a consistent upwelling that aggregates pelagics — thresher sharks circle the deep base during early morning dives, while big-eye trevally and rainbow runners school at mid-depth. The pinnacle's faces are festooned with gorgonian sea fans that reach 2 metres across, and the base is home to bumphead parrotfish in groups of 20 or more. Divers need to manage current and depth carefully but are rewarded with encounters that are hard to replicate elsewhere in the Visayas.
getThere: Banca from Panagsama Beach, Moalboal. Early morning departures before 07:00 give the best chance of thresher shark sightings. Operators combine with Sardine Wall for a second dive on the return.

name: South Drop
description: The southern tip of Pescador Island shelters a calmer face that rewards patient divers with the island's densest macro life. The wall here is more gradual than the western drop and is covered in leather corals, soft tree corals, and large barrel sponges that host cleaning stations busy with cleaner wrasse and cleaner shrimp. Giant moray eels are plentiful and often found resting in the open during daylight hours. The sand at the base of the wall at 25 to 30 metres is productive ground for hairy frogfish, robust ghost pipefish, and the occasional flamboyant cuttlefish. The reduced current compared to the north and west faces makes this suitable for divers still building confidence with Pescador's stronger conditions.
getThere: Accessed by banca from Panagsama Beach, Moalboal as part of a multi-dive Pescador trip. The south face is usually the second or third dive of the day when nitrogen management allows the shallower profile.

name: Kadidiri Wall
description: A sweeping vertical wall off Kadidiri Island draped in sea fans and black coral down to 40 m. Schooling fusiliers move in curtains above the drop-off, and the crevices shelter moray eels, ghost pipefish, and pygmy seahorses. Almost no diver traffic means undisturbed marine life behaviour.
getThere: Fly to Ampana via Palu or Luwuk, then take a public ferry or speedboat to Kadidiri Island (2 to 4 hours depending on vessel). Most dive resorts on Kadidiri provide boat transfers from Ampana.

name: Une-Une WWII Wreck
description: A Japanese WWII cargo vessel sits upright in 30 m off the volcanic Une-Une Island, largely unexplored and thickly encrusted with soft corals and sponges. The hold is intact and penetrable for experienced divers. Lionfish patrol the railings and schools of batfish hover over the superstructure.
getThere: Charter a local boat from Ampana or Katupat village. Une-Une is a 1.5 to 2 hour boat ride from Ampana. The wreck is not marked; a local guide with knowledge of the site is essential.

name: Katupat Macro Garden
description: A shallow sandy slope and rubble field off Katupat village that rewards slow, patient diving. Mimic octopus, flamboyant cuttlefish, blue-ringed octopus, and an exceptional density of nudibranchs make this one of Sulawesi's best muck diving spots. Night dives here regularly produce mandarin fish displays.
getThere: Short boat ride from Katupat village on Batudaka Island, accessible by public ferry from Ampana. Local dive guides in the village arrange site access.

name: Batu Daka Pinnacles
description: A cluster of submerged limestone pinnacles rising from 35 m to within 8 m of the surface off Batudaka Island. Currents funnel nutrient-rich water past sea fans, leather corals, and densely packed anthias. Napoleon wrasse and bumphead parrotfish make regular appearances. Intermediate drift experience recommended.
getThere: Boat from Kadidiri or Katupat (20 to 40 minutes). Conditions are most manageable at slack tide; arrange dive timing with the local operator in advance.

name: Cannibal Rock
description: A submerged rock formation off the southern tip of Rinca that consistently ranks among the best macro dives in Komodo National Park. The rock is smothered in colourful tunicates, sea apples, and crinoids, with ornate ghost pipefish, pygmy seahorses, and Coleman shrimp tucked into every crevice. Schools of sweetlips and bannerfish circle the shallows.
getThere: Accessed by liveaboard or day boat from Labuan Bajo (3 to 4 hours). The site is within Komodo National Park; a park entry permit and ranger fee are required. Most operators include fees in the package.

name: Yellow Wall of Texas
description: A dramatic vertical wall on the northwest side of Rinca named for the dense yellow soft corals that blanket its surface from 5 m down to beyond 40 m. Strong upwellings from the Indian Ocean bring cold, nutrient-rich water that feeds huge sea fans, gorgonians, and massive barrel sponges. Reef sharks and eagle rays patrol the blue water off the wall edge.
getThere: Liveaboard from Labuan Bajo or day trip by fast boat. The northwest coast of Rinca is exposed to swell from the Indian Ocean; entry by day boat depends on conditions. Liveaboard is the more reliable option for this site.

name: Toro Reef
description: A manta ray cleaning station off the east coast of Rinca where reef mantas queue above a shallow coral bommie to be groomed by cleaner wrasse. Schools of bumphead parrotfish and large dogtooth tuna feed on the adjacent reef. The site works best on incoming tide when current pushes from the channel.
getThere: Day boat from Labuan Bajo (2.5 to 3 hours) or liveaboard. Komodo National Park permit required. Most dive operators in Labuan Bajo include Toro Reef in standard Komodo itineraries.

name: Batu Bolong Rinca
description: A small rocky islet between Rinca and Komodo that rises from deep water, producing relentless current and one of the highest fish densities in the national park. Every surface of the rock is covered in corals and sponges. Grey reef sharks, giant trevally, and schooling barracuda are almost guaranteed. Experienced drift divers only when current is running full.
getThere: Day boat from Labuan Bajo (approximately 2 hours) or liveaboard. The site is dived at slack tide wherever possible; operators plan entries around tidal windows. Komodo National Park permit required.

name: Laje dos Dois Irmãos
description: A submerged basalt shelf stretching north from the iconic Dois Irmãos twin peaks, rising to 5 meters at its shallowest before dropping over a coral-draped wall to 30 meters. This is Fernando de Noronha's most reliable site for oceanic whitetip sharks, which cruise the blue water off the wall edge, drawn by the upwelling currents that funnel past the archipelago's northern tip. Bull sharks appear seasonally in the austral summer. Resident spinner dolphin pods from the Baía dos Golfinhos often work the current line above the shelf. The plateau itself is carpeted in brain coral and lettuce coral with dense populations of sergeant major, chromis, and queen angelfish.
getThere: Boat departure from Porto de Santo Antônio, approximately 15 minutes. All operators in Fernando de Noronha include this site in multi-dive day trips.

name: Gruta Azul
description: A flooded sea cave on the northwestern face of Ilha do Cabo Frio, one of Arraial do Cabo's most distinctive dives. At low tide an underwater arch at 6 meters leads into a cavern rising to an air pocket above, where indirect sunlight filters through and turns the water a luminous electric blue — the effect that gives the site its name. Visibility inside varies with upwelling pulses: on calm winter days the water can be 15 meters clear; in summer thermoclines can reduce it to 5. Spiny lobsters, moray eels, and bronze sweeper schools shelter in the ceiling cracks. Outside the cave a boulder slope drops to 20 meters with sea turtles, goatfish, and occasional Atlantic goliath grouper resting in the shade of large rocks.
getThere: Boat from Praia dos Anjos pier in Arraial do Cabo, approximately 20 minutes. Day trips depart 08:00 and 13:00. Cavern zone requires torch/light.

name: Ilha do Farol North Wall
description: The exposed northern face of Ilha do Farol — Lighthouse Island — where the cold South Atlantic Benguela-influenced upwelling hits Arraial do Cabo at full force, driving Arraial's most advanced and most rewarding dive. The wall begins at 8 meters and drops to 30, encrusted in massive gorgonian sea fans up to 2 meters across, orange cup corals, and sponge gardens that color the rock in violet and yellow. The current that scours the wall concentrates filter feeders and in turn attracts the larger animals: sea turtles, dusky grouper, Atlantic goliath grouper juveniles sheltering in gorgonian thickets, and occasional sightings of South American fur seals riding the current line in winter.

conditionsByMonth.suitRecommendation: 7mm wetsuit with hood and gloves; drysuit optional
7mm wetsuit with hood and gloves; drysuit optional

getThere: Boat from Praia dos Anjos pier, approximately 25 minutes. Recommended for advanced divers only due to strong current. Dive operators in Arraial do Cabo run guided trips; drift planning required.

name: Faial Caldeira Wall
description: The submerged outer flank of Faial's summit caldera drops from 5 m straight to over 40 m in a sheer volcanic wall blanketed with deepwater gorgonians, black coral bushes, and wide sponge gardens. Crevices shelter moray eels and Atlantic lobster; open water above the lip holds blue sharks that cruise the wall edge year-round. The wall is well protected from the dominant north swell in the channel between Faial and Pico, giving calmer conditions than exposed seamount dives. Visibility is typically 20 to 30 m. The dramatic relief, abundant macro life, and reliable shark sightings make this the best shore-accessible dive on the island.
getThere: Boat dive departing from Horta marina on Faial. Most dive centres on Faial run two boat dives daily to this site in summer. The dive centre of Horta is the main hub. Transit is under 15 minutes.

name: Pico Baixo
description: Pico Baixo is a submerged volcanic pinnacle off the south coast of Pico island, rising from 35 m to within 10 m of the surface. The topography creates acceleration corridors that concentrate pelagic fish and attract sperm whales feeding on squid in the deep water below the summit. Divers on the pinnacle encounter regular blue shark pass-bys, schools of Atlantic barracuda, and dense walls of chromis and damselfish. The base is colonised by black coral and deepwater gorgonians. This is one of the most reliable sites in the Azores for close encounters with sperm whales, which are observed resting at the surface nearby between deep foraging dives. Requires good buoyancy control due to variable surge on the pinnacle top.
getThere: Boat dive from Madalena on Pico island, the main port on the north coast. Dive operators in Madalena run regular trips to this pinnacle; transit time is approximately 20 to 30 minutes. Madalena is reached by ferry from Horta on Faial in 30 minutes.

name: Banco Dom João de Castro
description: Banco Dom João de Castro is a shallow submarine volcano between Terceira and São Miguel that has erupted as recently as 1720, leaving a summit just 14 m below the surface surrounded by a landscape of fresh lava flows, sulphurous vents, and pioneer reef colonisation. Hydrothermal gases bubble from cracks in the basalt, and the water carries a faint mineral warmth near the summit. Schooling barracuda and amberjacks patrol the shallower ridges while oceanic whitetip sharks and blue sharks sweep through in the blue beyond the crater rim.
